It’s an interesting spectacle. At this year’s conference in Brisbane, rightwing campaigner Monica Smit was deep in conversation with a Donald Trump impersonator, opera singers belted out the national anthem (the first verse, twice, for unknown reasons), senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price and her folk singer husband sang the anthem again, and Karl Stefanovic jokingly thanking CPAC for “rudely interrupting my unemployment”.

Stickers depicting Albanese with a Pinocchio nose, holding a brown burlap sack and a large blue sex toy emblazoned with “United Nations global citizen award” were found in the conference hall and in the men’s urinals. They carried no authorisation message, and did not appear to be officially endorsed by CPAC. Journalists were asked to wear a large red media accreditation lanyard emblazoned with “FAKE NEWS” – a gag CPAC has been pulling for years.

There was Barnaby Joyce handing out a few notes as props during his free-wheeling lecture about the value of money and the historical silver content of Roman coins, and seemingly every One Nation figure with a public profile (besides Farrer MP David Farley) wandering the halls.

Alongside boilerplate rightwing chaff like lower taxes, fiscal discipline and welfare, CPAC is a hotbed for hyper-engaged conservatives riled up on the red cordial of Sky After Dark. Last year’s event featured speakers criticising Peter Dutton as “Labor-lite”.
For all the twisting rabbit holes which various speeches followed, there was only really one prevailing theme which most boiled down to, and which this year’s conference revolved around.
Preferences.

To put it more accurately, the conference was about how Australia’s conservative right planned to boot Albanese and Labor out of office at the next election. With 94 Labor seats, and a splintered rightwing vote with Angus Taylor’s diminished Coalition opposition being whacked by Pauline Hanson’s surging One Nation, it’s a tall task.

To attend this year’s CPAC was to see Australia’s right recognising in real-time that they needed to figure out a way to cooperate; that for all the mocking of Albanese Labor as allegedly “the worst government in history”, conservatives face a third successive election defeat.

blocks.caption: Karl Stefanovic interviews Nationals leader Matt Canavan and One Nation leader Pauline Hanson. Photograph: Russell Freeman/AAP

blocks.text: CPAC, in messages to attenders, identified what it saw as the problem: “If you support One Nation but won’t preference the Coalition, or support the Coalition but won’t preference One Nation, you risk reinstalling Labor.”

But identifying the problem is only half the challenge. By the conference’s end, it wasn’t clear how parties of the right would, or could, cooperate. While Hanson signed a pledge to “to work together”, challenging Taylor and Canavan to follow suit, it came hours after she’d told the conference they shouldn’t trust the Coalition, and appeared to call the Liberal leader a “smarmy management consultant” unfit to replace Albanese.
Hanson at CPAC 2025 said she would “no longer be the bridesmaid” to the Coalition. She seems wedded to that, and said the ball was in Taylor’s court as to how their two parties would coexist.

Taylor had earlier dodged questions from Karl Stefanovic – to boos from the audience – about how the Coalition should cooperate with One Nation. He tried burnishing his conservative credentials by apologising for net zero, pandemic spending and immigration increases under Coalition governments, and later claiming “I know how to get Australia out of the hole Labor has put us in”, but it was clear many here had only come to see the Hanson show.
In previous years, the mood at the conference has been a decent weathervane indicating where the wind of the right is blowing.

blocks.caption: How close is One Nation to Australia's richest person? – video

blocks.text: In 2022, CPAC’s prevailing theme was urging the opposition to oppose the Indigenous voice referendum; a month later, the Nationals did, later followed by the Liberals. In 2025, alarmed Coalition speakers begged attenders for their loyalty in the face of One Nation’s rise, culture warriors railed against Sussan Ley’s leadership, and Canavan said the Liberals were on “the cusp” of dropping net zero. Within months, the Coalition split again, the Liberals dumped net zero and then Ley, and Hanson’s surge continued.

There’s some way to go before the next election, due by May 2028. The conservative side of politics still lays splintered. We’ll look back on this weekend to see if it was the start of the right’s rebuild, or just another forum to bag the prime minister.

articles.title: Marcos eyes deeper technology ties with Singapore
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said he is hoping that the Philippines and Singapore will enter into new partnerships, particularly in technology, once he steps down from office in 2028.

blocks.text: Published October 11, 2026 2:46pm
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said he is hoping that the Philippines and Singapore will enter into new partnerships, particularly in technology, once he steps down from office in 2028.
The Philippine leader noted that Singapore is leading the way when it comes to artificial intelligence (AI) in Southeast Asia.

“Hopefully by then, we will have entered into partnerships in the new areas that are becoming, the new opportunities that are being made available to us by the advent of new technology,” said Marcos in an interview with The Straits Times during his five-day work visit to the city-state.

“Of course, the biggest discussions now are being held over AI and Singapore has an important part to play in that because Singapore is actually, in our region, an industry leader when it comes to digitalization and AI,” he added.
Marcos earlier said that his visit to Singapore from October 7 to 11 would help prepare the Philippines for the industries of the future.
The President also said this latest working visit will build upon his previous trip to the country last July, where he engaged investors in digital infrastructure, AI, healthcare, and more.

“Singapore has been one of the biggest investors in the Philippines already. They have been very focused in the areas that they had wanted to develop but now we are exploring new areas, even areas such as health care, of course the digital economy, infrastructure, which is generally, traditionally, Singapore has not been involved before but they are coming into that now in the Philippines,” he told the Singaporean newspaper.
“This is a very, very important development for us and I think it's also of great benefit to Singapore,” Marcos added. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Ukrainian prisoners of war and defectors have been gathered into a Russian battalion to face Ukrainian forces — why? And how?
articles.summary: Russia has announced a battalion consisting of Ukrainian "volunteers." But veterans and former prisoners of war share very different accounts.

image.caption: Russian media reports say it has numerous military formations made up of former Ukrainian soldiersImage: Kaskad

blocks.text: Pavlo Oliynyk, 25, says he joined enemy forces to escape Russian captivity. Before his capture in the Donbas region in 2024, he was a senior lieutenant for Ukraine's armed forces.

As a prisoner of war (POW), he says he was electrocuted, beaten, and psychologically tortured. So when he received the offer to join the Maksym Kryvonis battalion — named after a famous 17th-century Cossack commander — he accepted.
Oliynyk says he wanted to use this opportunity to reach the front lines, so he could escape to Ukrainian-controlled territory. DW was able to contact Oliynyk through his lawyer.
'Ukrainian volunteers' consist mostly of POWs

Reports of Russian combat units consisting of Ukrainian prisoners of war and former servicemembers of Ukraine's armed forces began emerging in late 2022. Several detachments were initially formed and in August 2026, they were merged into the so-called "Ukrainian Volunteer Special Forces Brigade."

Of the individual units, the Maksym Kryvonis battalion has perhaps drawn the most public attention for having evidently taken part in combat. Its true size is unknown — Russian media reports claim about 200 fighters while available footage only suggests several dozen.

An investigative team of the Ukrainian public broadcaster Suspilne has identified over 30 members and confirmed they are all former Ukrainian servicemen, captured by Russian forces between 2023 and 2024.

blocks.caption: Pavlo Oliynyk says he defected to Russian forces in order to escape captivityImage: Privatarchiv

blocks.text: An 'imitation' of Russian legions fighting for Ukraine

Pavel Luzin, an expert for Russian foreign policy and defense at the Center for European Policy Analysis, believes these units are an "imitation" of the Russian Volunteer Corps and the Freedom of Russia Legion — units in the Ukrainian armed forces, consisting of Russian citizens — and an attempt by Moscow to distract from the fact that these units exist in the first place. Ukrainian intelligence services tend to agree.

"It bothers them that Russians would fight on Ukraine's side, but Ukrainians won't fight on Russia's side," Yevhen Shybalov, author and veteran of the war in Ukraine, tells DW. He adds that Russian troops have never tried to hide the fact that Russian volunteer units in Ukrainian ranks were the main reason Russian forces wanted to create Ukrainian units for their owns ranks.
Just how voluntary are these combat units?
In 2025, the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) reported that 95% of the released Ukrainian POWs interviewed reported torture or ill-treatment during Russian captivity.

Bill Wiley, executive director of the NGO Commission for International Justice and Accountability (CIJA), says that the physical and psychological state of the returned combatants raises serious doubts that their recruitment was voluntary. Mykhailo Savva of the Center for Civil Liberties, a Kyiv-based human rights organization, points to the criminal procedures running against several of the battalion members, which he says indicates that these suggest the combatants had switched sides voluntarily.

But where to draw the line between voluntary and involuntary recruitment? The war veteran and human rights activist Maksym Butkevych, who spent 28 months as a prisoner of war, says the conditions in Russian captivity make that line hard to distinguish. On the one hand, he says, there is a constant atmosphere of pressure, and on the other hand, it's not implausible that some prisoners defected out of ideological proximity.
How were Ukrainian prisoners made to join Russian forces?

Butkevych tells DW that between 2022 and 2023, all Ukrainian prisoners of war had received offers, "more or less persistently," to join the Russian army. In his case, he recounts, it was after he had been severely mistreated. "They showed us they could do anything they wanted to us," the veteran explains, "which was why we should agree to everything."

The veteran Shybalov reports similar experiences. He speaks of attempts to force confessions of war crimes, or to recruit members for Russia's intelligence services, and tells DW all prisoners were first interrogated and then made certain propositions under duress.

"You can torture people to get them to confess, but there comes the difficult moment when you need to give them a weapon," he says. "That's why it's more about psychological pressure, and forcing voluntary compliance."
Butkevych confirms these accounts with his own tales. But neither veteran has ever met someone willing to join Russian units, they say.
What happens after conscription?
Oliynyk, from the Maksym Kryvonis battalion, says he initially turned down multiple bids to join Russian forces. He says he only accepted the fourth offer so he could flee.

He claims he didn't sign official Defense Ministry paperwork, but a private contract with an individual offering military services. Afterwards, he says, he was brought to a room where he heard lectures and saw videos and photos he was later asked to retell.
Putin's foreign fighters
Control and mistreatment
He says fellow servicemembers in the Maksym Kryvonis battalion consisted both of those who had switched sides of their own volition, and those who had been forced.

In a video circulating online that appears to be of a trial in Ukraine, he also says that former Ukrainian POWs in the unit were followed and guarded by mercenaries of the private military company Redut. In the same video, he also speaks of beatings and torture, and receiving monthly wages in envelopes handed out by a member of Russia's military intelligence.

He tells DW he had been given a phone, but that he was too scared to call anyone in Ukraine because it was under constant surveillance. He denies having fought against Ukrainians, as he fled in March 2025 before his first deployment in the Donetsk province. After running across a field, he says he spent two days hiding from drones in basements and houses before making contact with Ukrainian fighters.
Now, Oliynyk has been in detention in Ukraine for nearly two years while authorities investigate possible treason. He has yet to be formally charged.
Sergey Nikitin contributed to this article, which originally appeared in Ukrainian.

articles.title: Marcos rejects claims of PH 'aggression' in WPS
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has rejected claims that the Philippines has been aggressive in its dealings with China amid continuing tensions in the West Philippine Sea, saying the country has only…

blocks.text: Published October 11, 2026 2:30pm

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has rejected claims that the Philippines has been aggressive in its dealings with China amid continuing tensions in the West Philippine Sea, saying the country has only been defending its territory and sovereign rights.
“We have never been aggressive in any way whatsoever,” Marcos said in an interview with The Straits Times during his five-day working visit to Singapore.
Marcos maintained that the Philippines was merely exercising its rights and protecting its territory, rejecting suggestions that its actions had contributed to tensions in the disputed waters.

“To say aggressive, aggressive is to go out and initiate some kind of conflict. We have never done that. We are there, we are sitting in our country, and all we do is defend our rights, defend our territory,” he said.

In 2016, an international arbitral tribunal in The Hague ruled in favor of the Philippines, invalidating China's sweeping claims over much of the South China Sea for having no legal basis under international law. Beijing has refused to recognize the ruling.
The Philippines lodged 296 diplomatic protests against China from 2022 to 2026, including 39 so far this year, according to the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA).

“So no, we have not been aggressive at all. We have been the point at which aggression is felt (more) than (in) any other country in the region. So I can assure you the aggression does not come from the Philippines,” Marcos said.
Marcos' remarks came amid continued reports of Chinese harassment of Philippine vessels in the West Philippine Sea.

In one of the latest incidents, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) reported that Chinese Coast Guard vessels obstructed and delayed the emergency medical evacuation of a Philippine Navy personnel from Ayungin Shoal.
Chinese vessels also reportedly interfered with a Philippine resupply mission to Ayungin Shoal on September 24, prompting condemnation from the United States Embassy in Manila.
The incidents were among the latest confrontations between Philippine and Chinese vessels in the disputed waters, where Beijing continues to assert its expansive maritime claims.

Despite the tensions, Marcos expressed openness to pursuing joint oil exploration with China, provided that both countries could agree on commercial arrangements without compromising their respective positions on territorial disputes.
Asked whether the Philippines remained willing to undertake joint oil exploration with Beijing, Marcos replied: “Yes, I absolutely do. I don't see why we cannot do that.”

“It is something that I think both countries would like to pursue and I think that if we keep it at a purely commercial level and do not enter into territorial conflicts and a resolution of who owns what and who belongs where, what law will apply,” he said.
“So long as we can come to an agreement on that and I don't see why we should not be able to have that partnership,” he added.
In August, Marcos said there was no definite timeline for the possible resumption of joint oil exploration talks between Manila and Beijing.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Robin Padilla, allied senators may skip Duterte impeachment trial over 'disregard for law'
articles.summary: Senator Robin Padilla on Sunday said he and his allied senators may skip the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte should there be what he described as disregard for the law.

blocks.text: Published October 11, 2026 2:26pm
Senator Robin Padilla on Sunday said he and his allied senators may skip the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte should there be what he described as disregard for the law.
Padilla told Super Radyo dzBB that senators in the minority bloc have not discussed skipping the impeachment trial, but such talks may happen soon.
“Wala pong ganoong usapan pero baka malapit na po (There has been no such discussion yet, but it may happen soon),” Padilla said.

He also opposed the Senate impeachment court’s ruling that the two-thirds voting threshold should be based on the number of senators who are “legally and factually participating in the impeachment proceedings.”

“Marami po kasing kagulat-gulat na mga nangyayari. Huwag na po nating i-identify kung na minority, majority kasi hindi maganda kapag impeachment tapos kami ay namomolitika pa. Kami po na naniniwala na sundin ang saligang batas,” Padilla said.

(There have been many surprising developments. Let us not identify whether we belong to the minority or majority bloc because it would not look good if we were seen as engaging in politics while an impeachment trial is ongoing. We believe in upholding the Constitution.)
“Ayaw naming mabaluktot ang batas. Kapag hindi tumigil ang pagbabaluktot ng batas ay baka baka dumating na punto na hindi na kami umattend,” he added.
(We do not want the law to be twisted. If this continues, there may come a point when we will no longer attend the proceedings.)
Earlier this week, Padilla and Senator Christopher “Bong” Go filed a petition asking the Supreme Court to declare null the Senate’s impeachment country’s ruling on the voting threshold.

In a petition for certiorari and prohibition, the senators and the Partido Demokratiko Pilipino-Lakas ng Bayan (PDP-Laban) asked the SC to issue a status quo ante order or a temporary restraining order directing the Impeachment court and the House of Representatives to refrain from excluding any senator from the count of “all members of the Senate” under the Constitution.
“The Constitution does not count only the Senators it finds convenient. It says ‘all,’ and ‘all’ has never meant ‘some.” Two-thirds of twenty-four is sixteen,” the petitioners said.
Villar joins majority bloc
On Thursday, Senator Mark Villar moved from the minority to the majority bloc after the Senate elected him to the Commission on Appointments and as chairman of the Senate Committee on Public Works.
For Padilla, the change should be seen in a positive light.
“Sa totoo lang po, sa ganitong bagay, kailangan positive ka lagi. Kasi masyado ng negative ang politika,” Padilla said.
(To be honest, in matters like this, you have to remain positive because politics has become too negative.)
“‘Yung paglipat ni (Senator) Mark (Villar) bilang legislative senator ‘yun. Hindi siya as senator-judge kasi diyan naman sa pagiging senator-judge wala namang minority, majority diyan,” he added.
(Senator Mark Villar’s transfer was in his capacity as a legislative senator, not as a senator-judge, because there is no minority or majority bloc in the impeachment court.)
Following the development, the majority bloc is now composed of 14 members, while the minority has 10 members — four of whom are currently not attending sessions.

Currently, Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta are detained over separate plunder charges, Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa is in hiding amid an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court, and Senator Loren Legarda has been absent for weeks due to health concerns and is currently abroad.
Padilla hoped that the minority bloc would not lose more members following Villar’s transfer.

“Wala pang nagpapaalam. Sana wala naman pero hindi naman namin ikasasama ng loob ‘yan kasi katunayan ho kakaunti lang naman talaga kaming nag-umpisang minority diyan. Sila lang naman ‘yung lumipat sa amin. So, hindi naman,” Padilla said.

(No one has informed us of any plans to leave. I hope no one does, but we will not take it against them because, in fact, we were only a few when we initially formed the minority bloc. They were the ones who later joined us.)—RF, GMA News

articles.title: Trump calls for replacing Ukraine’s Zelenskyy in tussle over diesel deal with Russia
articles.summary: 'I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president,' US President Donald Trump says

blocks.text: 'I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president,' US President Donald Trump says

US President Donald Trump on Saturday, October 11, called for Ukraine to replace its leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy and railed against Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil infrastructure, a day after announcing a diesel supply deal with Russia that had drawn a sharp rebuke from Zelenskyy.

In some of his harshest criticism yet of the White House, Zelenskyy linked the US lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel with a Russian attack on Saturday, October 10, that killed 20 people, including 3 children, in the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia.

A steep rise in global diesel prices, which followed the outbreak of the Iran war in February, has become a political liability for Trump’s Republican Party ahead of next month’s midterm elections, when opposition Democrats could gain control of one or both houses of Congress.
“I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump told reporters at the White House, saying Zelenskyy had hurt global diesel supplies with strikes on Russian refineries.
“He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world.”
Zelenskyy says diesel deal emboldens Russia

Earlier in the day, ZelZelenskyyensky said Trump’s announcement on Friday of the diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin had emboldened Moscow. Kyiv has instead urged Washington to pressure Moscow for serious negotiations to end the 4-1/2-year-old war.
The Russian government said on Saturday it had partially lifted a ban on diesel exports.
“Today, Russia said thank you for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said.

“Last night provided yet more confirmation that Russia perceives any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly keep fighting, that it can supposedly keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed.”
The southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia has been a regular target of Russian bombardment with strikes intensifying in the past few months.

On Saturday, a 6-year-old girl was among those killed in Zaporizhzhia when one strike reduced part of an apartment block to rubble. Her grandfather, Anatoliy Chumniy, stood sobbing over her body, laid on the ground in a white bag, after rescuers pulled it from the wreckage.
“Her birthday would have been at the end of the month,” he said through tears.
It was the third mass-casualty attack on Ukraine this week.

Nearly 80 civilians were killed in Russian strikes on Wednesday and Thursday, including at least 30 killed by a bomb in the eastern garrison city of Kramatorsk and 22 others by a missile in the town of Pryluky, about 130 km (80 miles) east of Kyiv.

The diesel deal was also criticized by US lawmakers, including one of Trump’s fellow Republicans, Representative Don Bacon, who said it was time to apply more sanctions that Congress had recently passed, not lift them.
Analysts said the agreement was unlikely to lead to sustained lower fuel prices, with the volumes still much lower than what Russia usually exports when its refineries are not under attack.
Britain vows to strengthen Russia sanctions

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke with Zelenskyy on Saturday and said Britain would strengthen its sanctions on Russia, according to a Downing Street spokesperson, who added that the two leaders would meet in person in the coming days.

The latest strikes followed talks between Ukrainian and European officials with US negotiators in Miami on Friday, which were aimed at developing a common proposal for ending the war, according to a person familiar with the discussions.
Trump announced the diesel deal while the negotiations were under way, a move Zelenskyy said had caught Kyiv by surprise.
The Ukrainian delegation was headed home on Saturday, presidential aide Dmytro Lytvyn was cited by the Interfax Ukraine news agency as saying.
Putin said after a call with Trump on Friday that an immediate resumption of ‌peace ⁠talks was unlikely, citing Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow.
US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner may visit Moscow within the next two weeks, Russian state news agency TASS reported on Saturday, citing a source.
In his remarks at the White House, Trump criticized Zelenskyy over the lack of a peace deal, while demanding an end to Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities.
“I said to him, ‘Do what you want. Don’t hit refineries. There’s plenty of targets. Don’t hit refineries.’ And he went out and he hit,” Trump said. “He better damn well stop.”
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals, but for some reason he never does,” he added. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Delhi braces for more protests as 'cockroach' group's leaders released
articles.summary: The leaders, including CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, had been detained when they arrived in Delhi on Saturday.

blocks.text: A court in the Indian capital has ordered the release of top leaders of the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) even as the city braces for protests for a second day with thousands of security personnel deployed and roads barricaded.

Abhijeet Dipke - who began the movement in May after India's Chief Justice likened some jobless young people to "cockroaches" - and other leaders had been detained on arrival in Delhi on Saturday to lead protests seeking electoral reforms.
Police refused them permission to protest and unprecedented curbs were in place to thwart the protesters from reaching the venue.
But thousands did try - media reports said 7,000 were detained and released late at night.
The CJP - which is not registered as a political party in India - is seeking electoral reforms just months before crucial state elections.
It has also demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists - which the Election Commission has denied.

On Sunday morning, the CJP lawyer Ratna Singh said she had been informed by the police that Dipke and two other senior CJP leaders - Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka - will be produced before the magistrate by the police seeking their remand "to maintain public peace".

She later posted on X that the three had been set free by the court "on the condition that they will not engage in breach of peace for one year" - it's not clear what that means and whether the CJP leaders can take part in protests.
Saturday saw dramatic developments as police officials boarded the flight to detain Dipke, Das and Ranka as their plane landed.

Police had refused permission for the protest to take place at Jantar Mantar, a landmark in the Indian capital, and the city was in a virtual lockdown to prevent the protesters from reaching the venue.
At least 45 metro stations were shut and Delhi's main railway stations were shut with major train services cancelled. Many protesters attempting to travel from outside were de-boarded en route.
Much of Delhi looked like a city under siege on Saturday, with roads barricaded and offices, shops and restaurants shut.
The day began with expectations of a major gathering at Jantar Mantar, but only a handful of protesters managed to reach the site before police swiftly removed them.
The road that the CJP had occupied for weeks earlier this summer seeking education reforms remained barricaded at both ends, guarded by thousands of police and paramilitary personnel.
The deployment continued through the day, but little happened at the site.
Elsewhere in the city, thousands of protesters still turned up, including activists and senior lawyers who were all detained.
Student leader Neha Bora tried to march from Dilli Haat to Jantar Mantar but was also stopped and taken away. They were all released later on Saturday.
One woman who managed to evade the police and reach Connaught Place told us: "In a democracy, everyone has the right to protest and to say if we are not happy.
"Peaceful protests have been there for ages. We are not living in pre-independent India. We request the government to let us protest."
The CJP has called for more protests on Sunday.
The row centres over a mammoth exercise to update electoral rolls nationwide - the commission has said it's a routine exercise to weed out dead, duplicate or ineligible voters.

At least 130 million voter names have been purged from the rolls so far and in many states, the exercise has been shrouded in controversy, with tens of thousands of people alleging they have been wrongly removed.
The CJP - and opposition parties - accuse Kumar of favouring Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the way the electoral rolls are being updated.
The Election Commission and the BJP have denied this.
The CJP first emerged as a major protest movement during weeks of demonstrations over the summer demanding education reforms and the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
The group stemmed from a joke made by Dipke in response to a remark by Chief Justice Surya Kant, who had likened jobless youngsters to "cockroaches". He later said the comments were misinterpreted.

Dipke, who previously worked with the opposition Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), had just completed a master's degree at Boston University when he posted a question on X in May: "What if all cockroaches come together?"
The post went viral, and the CJP was born. Momentum built around the movement which tapped into anger over unemployment, exam paper leaks and government accountability.
Their five-week-long protest ended in celebration for the protesters in July after the resignation of India's education minister.

articles.title: Manchester-based composer creates requiem to honour enslaved Africans
articles.summary:
David Önaç uses insurance documents for work funded by Lloyd’s of London after research uncovered its slavery links

A centuries-old insurance document detailing the trafficking of…

blocks.text: A centuries-old insurance document detailing the trafficking of enslaved Africans began with the words: “In the name of God, Amen.”

For Dr Errol Francis, the artistic director and chief executive of the arts and heritage charity Culture&, the contradiction was striking: an invocation of God in a document that treated human beings as cargo.
It gave him an unusual idea: what if the documents that once insured the trafficking of enslaved Africans could instead be used to create a requiem in their memory?
The new work, Atlantic Requiem, by the Manchester-based composer David Önaç, will premiere on Sunday at LSO St Luke’s in London, performed by the London Symphony Orchestra and BBC Singers.

Commissioned by Culture&, the project grew out of research into Lloyd’s of London, the historic insurance market whose members helped insure ships and enslaved Africans during the transatlantic slave trade.

Sponsored by Lloyd’s, the 40-minute, five-movement work brings together Catholic liturgy, historic insurance documents and testimony concerning the killing of an enslaved African woman aboard a ship in 1790.
Its musical language combines contemporary classical composition with jazz, gospel and other traditions that emerged on both sides of the Atlantic.
The performances, taking place during Black History Month, will be conducted by the Grammy award-winning conductor Malcolm J Merriweather.

“This is a really complicated situation in how religion is being used. Religion was used to convert the indigenous people then, the indigenous people often took up religion as part of emancipation,” Francis, who was a member of the steering group overseeing research into Lloyd’s historical involvement in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans, said.

“That was why I thought to myself, ‘Maybe we should write a Requiem Mass, because that would really bring out these contradictions and also use these documents for a different purpose than what they were intended for.’”

When Culture& approached Önaç about Atlantic Requiem, he jumped at the opportunity. “The styles that I’m interested in come from both sides of the Atlantic, so it just felt like I finally had this grand canvas on which I could explore these dual interests, allow the two styles to enrich one another,” he said.

blocks.caption: The account of John Cranston, preserved by the Newport Historical Society. Photograph: David Önaç/Guardian

blocks.text: For Önaç, who is of mixed heritage and hails from both sides of the Atlantic, the piece was an opportunity to explore longstanding questions about where he belongs.
“As a pianist, sometimes the piano itself and the layout or the geography is an inspiration to me,” he said.

“When you took the five black notes and two of the significant white notes from the other set, you got this seven-note blues scale, which is the product of the musical and cultural experience of enslaved Africans from the other side of the Atlantic.”

But while the work ultimately moves towards reconciliation and joy, some of its most harrowing passages confront the violence of enslavement directly. The second movement draws on a 1791 grand jury testimony concerning the killing of an enslaved African woman aboard the brig Polly, commanded by James DeWolf.

The testimony, preserved by the Newport Historical Society, records the account of John Cranston, a crew member who described a horrific incident during the ship’s voyage from Africa to the West Indies in 1791.
According to Cranston, an enslaved woman suspected of having smallpox was bound to a chair, gagged and thrown overboard on the captain’s orders, amid fears she would infect others aboard the ship.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Dr Errol Francis said the work acknowledges suffering but also survival. Photograph: Randerick Photography

blocks.text: “There’s bits in it that I get tearful even just talking about it,” Francis said. “It is about people who’ve passed away, but it’s also about the fact that we have survived this incredible trauma.”
For Önaç, the combination of the words and the music were at times so powerful that it felt overwhelming.

“The captain’s words were that he was sorry because he’d lost such a good chair,” he said. “I felt we needed to hear and see and experience what the human impact is here. What is the emotional impact? What is the loss of culture? What is the blindness to value?”

Lloyd’s has acknowledged its historical links to enslavement, and after the publication of the Underwriting Souls interactive archive, it announced its Inclusive Futures programme, aimed at supporting Black and ethnically diverse communities.
For some, this artistic project doesn’t go far enough. But Francis is careful to distinguish the requiem from important questions of financial redress.
“It’s not about reparations; it’s about an artwork that acknowledges the suffering, but also the survival of African people,” he said.
Önaç added that the requiem is not only a response to historical atrocities but a commentary on modern society.
“Everything’s so polarised and segregated and polemical right now, it seems to me, and I’ve tried to portray that in the black and white notes.
“It’s not just for then; it’s a commentary on now as well.”

articles.title: ‘You have a meeting’: the calendar phishing scam growing exponentially
articles.summary:
Appointment or renewal reminder appears in victims’ calendar to lure them into logging in to fake Google, Microsoft or PayPal page

You’re preparing for the week ahead and take a look at your…

blocks.text: You’re preparing for the week ahead and take a look at your Google calendar. There’s an entry for a meeting that you must have completely forgotten. The note that pops up when you click on it says you’ll be reviewing a project and includes a link to more details. Confused, you follow it to find out more; the website you land on asks for logon details, and you provide them.

Unfortunately, this was not a failure of your memory but a calendar phishing scam. You have handed your name and password to fraudsters who will sell it on in a batch with other people’s details, use it to break into your work email, or to persuade you that they are contacting you from your bank, or another institution.
Luke Wescott, a threat detection engineer at Sublime Security, says calendar phishing is still relatively new but the company has seen “exponential growth”.
The scam takes several forms, including a fake meeting, or a prompt to renew a service you pay for. In all, an entry appears in your electronic calendar.
It ends up there after scammers send an email to your work, or personal address, with a calendar request. It doesn’t matter if you miss it, or it ends up in your spam folder.

blocks.caption: Fake notifications of an auto-renewal are common to persuade people to respond and hand over personal details. Photograph: Sublime Security

blocks.text: “Calendar apps, such as Google Calendar, can add invitations automatically without users even accepting them,” Wescott says. “So scammers don’t even need you to open an email.”

And while you may not look twice at one from someone whose name you do not recognise, when something turns up in your calendar you may treat it differently. “It can create a borrowed credibility by showing up in the same place as your dentist appointment or a weekly 1:1 with your boss,” he says.

Max Gannon, an intelligence analysis manager at the cybersecurity company Cofense, says some scammers are using legitimate platforms such as Zoom to send the invitations, making them look more convincing to the recipients, and to security software.
“That makes it really hard to block,” he says. “Even AI-backed blockers struggle.”
If you set up something to filter out invitations from these platforms, he says “that would also block any legitimate meeting invitations”.
What it looks like
You will receive an email and see an entry in your calendar. The titles vary: examples seen by the Guardian include fake meetings, notifications of voicemail messages, and software renewals.

Wescott says this is standard. “We typically see stuff like ‘New voicemail received’, ‘Payment receipt confirmation – $298.99’, ‘PayPal unusual activity’ warnings, ‘Your auto-payment will be processed within 24 hours’, and invitations to bid on a contract,” he says.

blocks.caption: Sometimes the calendar phishing scam uses fake voicemail notifications. Photograph: Supplied

blocks.text: Gannon says the invitation could look like it has come from within your company. “If they want to they could make it look like an internal invitation,” he says. “They can customise the content, may be adding the logo of your company.”
The event description will typically contain a link, or a phone number.

Wescott adds: “Either they want you to click a link to a fake login page like Microsoft, Google or PayPal, and enter your password, or to call a ‘support’ number to cancel a charge that never actually happened.”

Until you click on this, or make a call, you are not compromised. The scammers do not have access to everything in your calendar – they are just trying to lure you to a place where you will hand over your details.
As Wescott says, “it sounds familiar to typical phishing, it’s the same technique, just using a different delivery method”.
What to do
Don’t panic if you see an unexpected meeting or reminder in your calendar. Treat it as you would an unexpected email and don’t click on the link.
“My number one advice is people just need to be paranoid,” Gannon says. “It doesn’t matter if the invitation has come from someone two desks down, you’ve got to be suspicious of everything.”
Wescott advises turning off automatic accepting. In Google Calendar you can go into settings and opt to only accept invitations from known senders, or when you have accepted.
He adds: “Don’t click ‘decline’ on suspicious invites as it can tell the sender that your address is ‘live’. Instead, delete or report it as spam/junk.”

articles.title: ‘We need less point scoring’: What party conference season taught us about UK climate action
articles.summary:
Tories plan to scrap low-carbon housebuilding, Greens back new nuclear reactors, and Labour put oil-drilling decisions on hold

New homes could be built without solar panels, heat pumps and…

blocks.text: New homes could be built without solar panels, heat pumps and high-grade insulation, leading to higher household bills if the Conservative party wins the next general election.
Kemi Badenoch made scrapping the future homes standard (FHS) one of the central planks of her bid to become the next prime minister at the Tory party conference this week.

The announcement gained little attention compared to her inheritance tax bombshell, but it would have more far-reaching impacts on a greater number of people. The UK is in need of approximately 6m new homes and failing to equip them with efficient and low-carbon energy sources would doom households to higher bills for decades to come.

The Tories quoted estimates of £30,000 for new-build houses, but the real cost is likely to be much less. Installing heat pumps, solar panels, batteries and insulation costs about £5,000 to £8,000 at the point of building – a figure estimated in 2024 when energy prices were much lower – to save more than £1,300 a year on bills, a saving likely to be substantially higher now. To retrofit homes after building would cost more than £20,000.

Jan Rosenow, a professor of climate and energy policy at the University of Oxford, said: “Every home constructed today that runs on fossil fuels is a liability for the occupants. It also results in investor uncertainty and disrupts the supply chain that has been gearing up for this. What we need is less political point scoring and more long-term clarity.”

blocks.caption: Construction workers install solar panels on a house in the north-east of England. Photograph: Washington Imaging/Alamy

blocks.text: Housebuilders have been among the biggest donors to the Conservative party, though this has fallen off in recent years. And according to the UK Green Building Council (UKGBC), the construction industry is well prepared for the FHS and will have to implement the policy before the next general election, so scrapping it is of little benefit.

Simon McWhirter, the chief executive of UKGBC, said: “The housebuilding industry has spent years preparing for the introduction of the FHS, investing in skills, supply chains and new products. Reversing course would … risk slowing progress towards building the homes that people want and need.”

Badenoch’s housebuilding plans are only part of a torching of the Tories’ green policies. Despite the crisis of sewage and farm pollution in the UK’s rivers and beaches, and the dramatic drop in wildlife, the party would abolish the Environment Agency and Natural England.

The party’s U-turn on environmental issues and net zero was contrary to what voters wanted, said Robbie MacPherson, Kennedy scholar at Harvard University and the former head of the UK’s all-party parliamentary group on climate. “No winning political strategy, after years of fossil fuel-driven energy price spikes and a summer of climate breakdown, can include environmental regression.
“Voters won’t reward politicians who want to kill employment opportunities, spurn economic growth and fail to keep Britain safe.”

While the Conservatives spent their party conference burning their green credentials, an equally unexpected U-turn came from the Green party, which resolved last weekend to abandon its long-held opposition to nuclear power.

blocks.caption: Zack Polanski at the party conference in Bournemouth. The Greens will still prioritise renewable energy but MPs will now support new nuclear reactors. Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News

blocks.text: Although the party would still prioritise renewable energy, Green MPs could now support new reactors, in recognition of their potential role in low-carbon generation.
after newsletter promotion

Paul Dorfman, Bennett scholar at the University of Sussex and the chair of the Nuclear Consulting Group thinktank, said: “The Green party has taken a wrong turn on nuclear and this will lose them significant grassroot support and votes.

“With 20-plus-year construction times, repeated delays and huge cost overruns, new nuclear diverts scarce resources from faster options. Renewables, storage, efficiency and stronger grids can deliver much more for every pound spent.”

The battle between the Green party and the Labour party in this week’s Holborn and St Pancras byelection is likely to be repeated during the general election, where the Greens could be the main challengers in urban Labour strongholds.

Responding to Sagal Abdi-Wali’s win for Labour, Greenpeace UK’s head of politics, Ami McCarthy, said: “Abdi-Wali has shown that voters are putting their trust in Labour, but the Green party increased its share of the vote and remains a serious challenger. As extreme heat becomes a regular threat and droughts extend for much of the year, concern about climate change is on the rise and cannot be ignored.”

At Labour’s conference, Andy Burnham made only passing references to the climate, pollution crises and nature. He announced a publicly owned body to invest in the energy grid, alongside the privatised National Grid, which has been criticised for slow progress on upgrades. There was also a nod towards localised support for nature with a community fund for planting 500,000 trees across England.

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham made only passing references to the climate, pollution crises and nature at the Labour conference. Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPA

blocks.text: McCarthy said: “Voters will be comparing Labour with other parties that have a clear plan to lower energy bills and tackle the climate crisis rather than with the fantasies of the Conservatives and Reform. Labour has a clear plan but needs to deliver it – starting with a full-throated rejection of any scramble for fossil fuels in the North Sea.”
The decision on the future of the Rosebank and Jackdaw drilling sites was reportedly postponed for the byelection, and McCarthy said it would “truly define this government’s legacy on climate”.

Failure to recognise and tackle the damage caused to the UK by a summer of record heat and drought would prove costly, campaigners warned. A record El Niño weather system is brewing, super-charged by global heating and likely to bring heatwaves, droughts and floods to key agricultural areas, pushing millions into hunger and raising food prices globally.

Rosie Downes, the head of campaigns at Friends of the Earth, said: “With El Niño bringing a wetter and stormier winter season to the UK, we desperately need to see some parties getting back in touch with reality. The government must translate its words into action that delivers for people and the planet.”

articles.title: Sugarfree’s ‘Dramachine’ gets the classic vinyl treatment
articles.summary: For years, fans have clamored for vinyl releases of Sugarfree’s albums. Their contemporaries have been rolling out remastered editions of their catalogs, and Sugarfree surely deserves the same.

blocks.text: For years, fans have clamored for vinyl releases of Sugarfree’s albums. Their contemporaries have been rolling out remastered editions of their catalogs, and Sugarfree surely deserves the same.

items: Ebe Dancel's 'Baliktanaw' album provided comfort during the pandemic by revisiting his songs from Sugarfree with stripped-down arrangements, focusing on themes of loss and healing.
While Sugarfree's debut album 'Sa Wakas' was released on vinyl, it was criticized for poor sound quality, prompting plans for remastered releases of their next two albums by Backspacer Records.
Jett Galindo, an experienced mastering engineer, is set to improve the sound quality of Sugarfree's albums, ensuring that the emotional dynamics of the music are preserved and enhanced.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

During the pandemic, Ebe Dancel’s Baliktanaw album became a quiet companion for many of us. Dancel revisited the songs he wrote for his former band Sugarfree, stripping the arrangements to acoustic guitar, keyboards, and strings. The songs, and Dancel’s earnest vocals, soothed the ache of disconnection, of loss and longing, while the world stayed home.

Sugarfree never claimed the title of patron band of loss and longing. The bands that came before them and their own contemporaries also wrote about heartbreak, approaching the difficult topic with irony, anger, novelty, or social commentary, usually with big, audacious gestures. Dancel went small.

His songs are confessional monologues: plainspoken, conversational, raw. They hang on small details that put you in a specific time and place. They leave you with a feeling that is hard to shake. Listen to the tender “Tulog Na,” or the grief that fills a messy room of memories in “Kwarto.” Dancel’s best songs, however, do not stand in place. They never wallow in grief. There is always movement in them, a search for healing, a step past the hurt.

The band’s debut, “Sa Wakas,” did make it to vinyl, and it was a letdown. The sibilance hisses, the sound is muddy, and the dynamics are flattened. It sounds like an album that went direct to vinyl without anyone stopping to master it for the format.

That major oversight is being corrected. Indie OPM label Backspacer Records is releasing the band’s next two albums on vinyl: Dramachine and Tala-Arawan. The vinyl masters are by Jett Galindo, and the choice is perfect.

Galindo grew up in Quezon City and earned a psychology degree from the Ateneo before leaving for Berklee to study audio engineering. In 2013, she became the assistant to legendary cutter Doug Sax at The Mastering Lab in Ojai, California. Sax founded the first independent mastering studio in 1967, and Galindo calls him “the grandfather of mastering.” He taught her to cut vinyl.

She then spent nearly a decade at The Bakery, a mastering house on the Sony Pictures lot where she mastered and cut vinyl for Green Day’s Revolution Radio, the La La Land soundtrack, and Billie Eilish’s Hit Me Hard and Soft. Her credits also include Barbra Streisand, Weezer, Pink Floyd, and Neil Young. She now runs her own studio, Jett Galindo Mastering, in Los Angeles.

What she brings to Sugarfree is her mentor’s creed: less is more, and stay faithful to the music. She also knows the format’s traps. In interviews, she has named the hazards that make vinyl cutting tricky, and sibilance tops the list. That is the very flaw that sank Sa Wakas.

I heard a test pressing of Dramachine, and the difference is immediate. The soft-loud dynamics, the album’s emotional driver, are intact and in balance. The quiet passages breathe, and the loud ones land without flattening everything around them. The clarity puts Dancel’s voice where it belongs, front and center, every word legible. This is how a classic album should sound.

It has been a busy year for Backspacer. Since its first OPM release during the pandemic, the self-titled album of indie darling Peryodiko, the label has collected a string of Awit Awards and earned the respect of vinyl collectors for its design, packaging, and mastering. Its catalog now includes emerging acts, legacy pop singers, P-pop superstars, and elder statesmen of rock and jazz.

Robert Tuazon, who runs the label with his wife Tasha, talks about the work like a fan, not a businessman. “As music fans, this gives us the ultimate pride and satisfaction,” he said in an early interview with this writer. “So as long as we can accommodate them, we would love to keep continuing to press more and more OPM records on vinyl.”
That leaves one piece of unfinished business. Tuazon is hoping for a second crack at Sa Wakas, with Galindo at the board.
I say give it to them. The album that started it all deserves to sound like the classic that it is. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Winner in life: Carlos Yulo ready to take on new challenges
articles.summary: Even after completing his golden collection, Carlos Yulo has no plans to slow down anytime soon, pursuing not only success in gymnastics but also opportunities to grow and develop as an individual

blocks.text: WINNER. Carlos Yulo in action for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games.
Edgar Su/Reuters
Even after completing his golden collection, Carlos Yulo has no plans to slow down anytime soon, pursuing not only success in gymnastics but also opportunities to grow and develop as an individual
MANILA, Philippines – Carlos Yulo has nothing more to prove.

He has won gold medals in almost every major competition, capturing two at the Olympics, three at the World Championships, 12 at the Asian Championships, five in the World Cup Series, nine at the Southeast Asian Games, and, most recently, two at the Asian Games to complete his collection.
And yet, Yulo has no plans to slow down anytime soon. He continues to chase success in gymnastics while looking for opportunities to grow as an individual.

“There’s always more to improve on, more challenges to take on, and more to learn. God gives us unlimited challenges and we really have to embrace them. If His blessings are also unlimited, why should we hold back when it comes to giving our best to ourselves and, of course, to Him? For me, it’s really all about gaining experiences,” said Yulo in a mix of Filipino and English.

“It doesn’t matter how many times I fall or how many times I lose. Even when I was younger, winning was never really the main goal — it’s the experiences we gain in life that we carry with us as we grow older.”

blocks.caption: Winner in life: Carlos Yulo ready to take on new challenges

blocks.text: After the Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Yulo immediately returned to training. He, his younger brother Eldrew, and Juancho Miguel Besana are training in Antibes, France, for the World Championships in Rotterdam, Netherlands, from October 17 to 25.

Although he has won titles across major competitions, the 26-year-old looks to defend a world title for the first time in his career. He is eyeing another gold following his vault triumph at the 2025 World Championships in Jakarta, Indonesia, where he also won bronze in floor exercise.
Yulo also has his sights set on the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, where he is the defending champion in both the floor exercise and vault.

“There’s still a lot,” said Yulo when asked what more he wants to achieve. “Of course, the Olympics will always be one of them. And when my gymnastics career comes to an end — which I think is still quite a long way off — I really want to help young children by giving them the proper knowledge about gymnastics and sharing my experiences, both from my career and from my journey through life. I really want to give back to them.”
“I hope that one day, we’ll see many Filipino gymnasts competing internationally.”
Beyond his gymnastics aspirations, Yulo is also entering an important new chapter in his life as he prepares to marry his longtime girlfriend, Chloe San Jose.
Yulo proposed to San Jose in December 2025, but they kept their engagement private until shortly after his golden double at the Asian Games, when they decided to announce it publicly.
Sure, juggling wedding preparations while staying focused on his gymnastics will not be easy, but it is anew journey that Yulo is embracing with open arms.

“I’m always happy to take on these challenges in my life. It’s not going to be always smooth. I’m really, really happy and grateful for whatever challenges the Lord gives me, and I think this is one of His challenges for me. I feel like I’m not alone because I have so many people who love me,” said Yulo.

At the heart of his support system is San Jose, whom Yulo credits as one of the people who helped propel him to success. His decision to give her two engagement rings, symbolizing his two Olympic gold medals, reflects the significance of their relationship and the place she holds in his life.
“I didn’t just win in sports; I also won in life,” Yulo said. – Rappler.com

blocks.text: Live
Leaders of the youth-led protest movement had been detained ahead of a large protest in Delhi calling for India's election commissioner to step down. Fresh protests have been called. Follow DW.

blocks.text: What you need to know
Here are the latest developments from India on Sunday, October 11:

items: The CJP's Abhijeet Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das ordered released after nearly 24 hours of detention
Indian media reports cite Delhi Police officials as saying thousands of detained protesters were released
The CJP called for a fresh protest on Sunday

blocks.text: Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
October 11, 2026
'Cockroach' leaders ordered released from detention, party says
An executive court in Delhi has ordered the release of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke and other leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, the youth-led movement said on Sunday.
The three were detained ahead of a large protest in Dehli on Saturday and appeared in court earlier on Sunday after being in detention for nearly 24 hours.
Earlier, the CJP had alleged the leaders were being detained at an undisclosed location and did not have access to their lawyers.
On Saturday evening, the CJP issued a fresh call for a march to New Delhi's Jantar Mantar on Sunday.
"We're not backing down! We will march to Jantar Mantar again tomorrow," Ajinkya Shinde, the CJP's interim protest leader, said at a press conference.
The exact number of demonstrators detained during the protest could not be immediately verified.
Shinde told reporters that over 15,000 people, including students, had been detained across India.
The Hindu newspaper, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that 2,500 demonstrators were detained in Delhi on top of 1,000 people picked up in overnight preventive measures ahead of the protest.
Indian media reports cite Delhi Police as saying that all detainees had been released later on Saturday.

articles.title: Ben Roberts-Smith attends Canberra event honouring Australian troops who served in Afghanistan
articles.summary:
Anthony Albanese speaks at Australian War Memorial event commemorating 25th anniversary of country’s involvement in the conflict

  • Get our

blocks.text: Anthony Albanese has honoured Australian troops who served in Afghanistan, using the 25th anniversary of the country’s involvement in the conflict to describe their heroism as a fight for “who we are as a people”.

The prime minister joined hundreds of veterans, family members and dignitaries at a commemoration of the start of the campaign in Canberra on Sunday, with nation’s most decorated living soldier and accused war criminal Ben Roberts-Smith among the crowd at the Australian War Memorial.
“In New York, fires were still burning at Ground Zero from the September 11 attacks a month earlier. The world felt upended,” Albanese said of the start of Operation Slipper.
“Though it would change so devastatingly a year later in Bali, it was not yet directly our fight.
“Yet Australia did what is so resolutely in our nature. We went to support our friend and ally.
“We went because we saw what was at stake, and we went on the principle that September 11 was an attack on a way of life that belonged just as much to us.”

He said the more than 35,000 defence force members deployed over the following two decades did so because the very freedoms “that are at the heart of who we are as a people and a nation were under threat”.
Roberts-Smith, who denies the allegations against him, attended the event alongside family members and supporters, as well as former prime ministers John Howard, Tony Abbott and Scott Morrison.
The governor general, Sam Mostyn, and the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, were also present in the bright sunshine.

Roberts-Smith was awarded Australia’s highest military honour – the Victoria Cross – for his service in Afghanistan, but now faces accusations he murdered five unarmed detainees during his deployment.
The former Special Air Service regiment corporal sat alongside his partner, Sarah Matulin, after a judge agreed to vary his bail conditions to allow him to visit Canberra.
Deployments to the Middle East continued until withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021.

US troops left a few months later after signing an agreement with the Taliban, who swiftly returned to power and reintroduced authoritarian control, including strict suppression of women and girls’ rights.
Some 47 Australian personnel died as a result of their service and 263 were wounded, while thousands more allied soldiers were killed.
Tens of thousands of civilians were also estimated to have been killed during the war.
Despite the controversy over Australia’s military involvement in Afghanistan and its legacy, the troops who served on the ground remain intensely proud of what they achieved.
after newsletter promotion
Soldier Mathew Bell was deployed in 2012, aged 24, with his infantry battalion to a forward operating base in Afghanistan’s “badlands” west of Tarinkot.
More than a decade after he returned to Australia, Bell remembers his unit’s work with a sense of honour and accomplishment.
“We changed that little part of Afghanistan, that little part of the world for good,” the former lance corporal, now 38, said.
Bell said girls were able to attend school, medical services were rolled out to villages and “there was freedom”.
“Not the oppression we’re seeing now under the Taliban government,” the father of two said.
“Our role was essentially to go out on either vehicle-mounted patrols or foot patrols, out among the local population through the desert, through the green zone, keeping the Taliban at bay.
“It was a hot area. Once you stepped over that line in the sand, like, that was Taliban territory.”
One of Bell’s close mates was badly wounded in a roadside bomb explosion and on more than one occasion, his section was pinned down by sniper fire.
Services were also held at the Anzac Memorial in Sydney’s Hyde Park, at Melbourne’s Shrine of Remembrance and other sites around the country.
Australians who served in the Afghanistan War were deployed in various roles and missions contributing to reconstruction efforts, democratic governance, training and humanitarian aid.
Operation Slipper was followed between 2015 and 2021 by Operation Highroad and the Kabul airlift in August 2021.
