articles.title: Two Carlton players treated in hospital after needing care for ‘separate circumstances’
articles.summary:
Club issues brief statement about Lachie Cowan and Will Hayward, saying latter suffered minor cut to head after a fall

Carlton football…

blocks.text: Carlton football club has said two of its players, Lachie Cowan and Will Hayward, required treatment in hospital on Sunday morning in “separate circumstances”.

The club released a statement on Sunday after reports in several media outlets that unnamed players had been taken to hospital by ambulance after a night out. Guardian Australia contacted Carlton seeking comment on the reports.

blocks.caption: Will Hayward in action in August. Photograph: Rob Prezioso/AAP

blocks.text: The statement said Cowan had “received medical treatment and underwent observation, before being discharged a short time later” but did not provide any more information about the circumstances.
Hayward was also admitted to hospital on Sunday morning.
“Will Hayward experienced a minor cut to the head after a fall, and admitted himself to hospital where he received stitches before being discharged,” Carlton said.
“The club has been in regular contact with both players, with priority for their wellbeing and both players have now received the necessary care relating to their separate circumstances.”

articles.title: US justice department investigates TV networks over Trump pool coverage
articles.summary: The White House had blocked access for CNN, MS Now and Politico, leading them to restrict pool coverage.

blocks.text: The US justice department (DoJ) has said it is investigating several TV networks over whether they broke federal competition laws when they recently suspended pool coverage of President Donald Trump.
Last month, five networks paused their presidential coverage for several days in response to the Trump administration withdrawing the credentials of reporters from CNN, MS Now and Politico.

The justice department asked ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News to hand over communications related to the pool and said that the boycott could violate the Sherman Act, referring to a law that bars companies from engaging in monopolistic business practices.
Pool members usually share their material with the wider media.
A DoJ spokesperson said: "The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these ​news organisations have violated the antitrust laws."
The television networks have not yet commented.
Trump blocked CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House last month after accusing the organisations of writing "fiction or lies" about his team.
The White House later reinstated their access after a ruling from a judge. The three outlets had sued the Trump administration, arguing the restricted access violated their First Amendment rights.

The First Amendment forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.
The Trump administration has taken a number of legal actions against news publications in the US, including lawsuits over coverage of the president.
In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association.

The same month, the Trump administration moved to bar Associated Press (AP) reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America". AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing.

articles.title: ‘Restore the authority’: the challenge for the BBC’s new director of news
articles.summary:
Rachel Jupp takes role as corporation grapples with digital transformation, a cash crisis and its public service role

With looming job cuts and an ongoing pay dispute, there has not been…

blocks.text: With looming job cuts and an ongoing pay dispute, there has not been much to smile about for BBC journalists working in “the pit” – their pet name for the newsroom deep in the belly of New Broadcasting House.

On Monday afternoon, however, they were greeted by a grinning figure conducting a tour of the news floor. She was Rachel Jupp, the BBC’s newly appointed director of news and current affairs. Jupp engaged in a series of polite if brief conversations with her new troops.

It was a small but welcome gesture for a newsroom that had been desperate for a sense of direction from a new, permanent leader. The shock resignation of Deborah Turness, Jupp’s predecessor, was almost a year ago. Frustration has grown among journalists awaiting a grand plan.
“We just need a set direction of travel,” said one. “A north star, as startups call it. Lay out a timeline and tell everyone what cuts are coming and what needs to be done.”

Beyond the small talk, figures at all levels of the corporation acknowledge that Jupp faces a huge task. Running the world’s most scrutinised newsroom is a tall order at the best of times, even without the turmoil over pay and job losses.

blocks.caption: Rachel Jupp faces a huge task, say BBC figures across the corporation.  Photograph: BBC/PA

blocks.text: Jupp takes the helm at BBC News as it is gripped by an angst-ridden debate about the place of its journalism in an increasingly digital world. It is one she has been tasked with resolving.

It is a world in which the BBC’s hallmarks of impartiality and authority – and focus on television and radio news – are pitted against content creators and a myriad of other established media brands converging to reach audiences via a handful of smartphone apps.

Inside BBC News, a series of announcements about show closures and strategy shifts have fuelled a “clicks v public service” debate. There are competing views over how the BBC should adapt its content for commercially driven digital platforms favoured by younger audiences – while sticking to the corporation’s founding principles of informing the public.

“I’ve heard the DG [director general, Matt Brittin] and [the deputy director general, Rhodri Talfan Davies] have been saying to people that they want the new director of news to restore the authority of BBC News,” said Roger Mosey, the former head of BBC TV News.

“I think that’s what a lot of us have been arguing for. BBC News does all sorts of good things and it’s generally an impartial and fair service. But it hasn’t been able to translate the authority of the really big brands of TV and radio into an online world.”

Those concerned that the corporation is at risk of losing its bearings point to a BBC website piece about penis fillers or recent social videos of reporters holding cheap mics, content creator-style. Meanwhile, they fear flagship shows such as the Today programme or the 10 O’Clock News, which continue to attract large audiences, have not been nourished or championed online.

Those pushing for a faster embrace of new platforms say it is clearly where audiences are heading and the broadcaster’s requirement to cater for everyone is at the heart of its public service remit. As one BBC figure put it: “Rachel’s task and challenge is to show how we can do what every news organisation is having to do – go digital, without becoming a value-free click factory.”
Above all else, Jupp’s willingness to take on this precarious task is why she was handed such a big promotion.

While the BBC’s relatively new director general, Matt Brittin, inherited many of the cuts being announced across the BBC, Jupp’s appointment was in his hands. At an all-staff call this week, he said he wanted the organisation to be “a bit more Elvis – a little less conversation, a little more action”. In Jupp, Brittin believes he has found one of his best Elvis impersonators, willing to make changes for the digital age.

Jupp triumphed from a shortlist of four candidates. There was a recognition that one of her competitors, Jonathan Munro, had managed to avoid any major crises as the interim head of BBC News – an achievement not to be underestimated, given recent criticisms.
after newsletter promotion

However, the job came down to Jupp and Esme Wren, the editor of Channel 4 News. Wren was recognised as a formidable champion of journalists and journalism, but the conclusion was that the BBC’s news machine produces plenty of high-quality, award-winning material.

blocks.caption: Matt Brittin, the director general, is said to have stated that he wanted the new director of news ‘to restore the authority of BBC News’. Photograph: Carl Court/Getty Images

blocks.text: While Jupp had not run a big organisation before – something Brittin had been looking for – the director general believed Jupp had two important qualities. The first was solid editorial judgment – a requirement after bruising criticisms over a Gaza documentary that had to be pulled and a spliced-together Trump speech that led to a multibillion-dollar lawsuit.

Jupp had been tasked with overseeing the BBC’s documentary and long-form journalism content after the Gaza row, so was seen as someone who would safeguard the BBC’s authority as it pushed deeper into digital content.

Her second quality was an appetite for transformation, the buzzword for the mammoth task of translating the BBC’s journalism on to new digital platforms without losing its authority – seen, at best, as a work in progress. Jupp has also been at the heart of the BBC’s use of generative AI, and Brittin – a former Google executive – believes this can have a bigger role if used in the right way.
It also helped that Jupp could start almost immediately, given the pace at which a cash crisis is forcing the BBC into big, strategic choices.

Jupp also begins her tenure with another underrated advantage: she is genuinely liked by close colleagues and respected by journalists who have worked with her in previous roles at Channel 4 News, Newsnight and Panorama.

As her tour of the pit illustrated, starting with the support of her staff is seen as essential as she embarks on a transformation of BBC News that will include some difficult and unpopular decisions.

articles.title: Retrofit schools and consider moving exams to beat extreme heat, says teaching union leader
articles.summary:
NEU’s Daniel Kebede says earlier start times and longer summer breaks may be needed to help pupils and teachers

Schools should consider changing start and finish times, reordering holidays…

blocks.text: Schools should consider changing start and finish times, reordering holidays and moving exams from the summer months in an effort to adapt to the UK’s increasingly severe heatwaves, according to the leader of the country’s biggest education union.

Daniel Kebede, the general secretary of the National Education Union (NEU), said this summer’s repeated bouts of extreme heat had a devastating impact on teachers and pupils, as classroom temperatures topped 40C and hundreds of thousands of young people were sent home.

Speaking to the Guardian, Kebede called on the government to roll out a mass retrofitting programme to ensure schools – which he said had been built “for a different climate” – were better equipped to deal with extreme heat ahead of next summer’s El Niño-charged temperatures.
And he said it was time for a national conversation about other measures that could help schools adapt to the reality of a rapidly warming climate.

“There needs to be a really serious discussion about how we make sure there is the continuity of education in this changed climate,” he said. “You might want to consider moving the school year around, or having a longer summer holiday – in hot countries they tend to have a longer summer holiday. You might consider an earlier start and earlier finish … and perhaps we don’t want exams to be happening in the hottest part of the year.”
Kebede said he had been inundated with messages from teachers during this summer’s heatwaves urging the union to help.

“The last time I felt that level of panic in the profession was during the Covid pandemic,” he said. “I was being routinely contacted by members in distress … they felt there was a real risk and danger to themselves and to their pupils.”

blocks.caption: Daniel Kebede: ‘There needs to be a really serious discussion about how we make sure there is the continuity of education in this changed climate.’ Photograph: PA/Alamy

blocks.text: At least 760,000 schoolchildren in England and Wales missed lessons owing to school closures during this summer’s June heatwave – one in five in the UK in the space of a few months – with pupils missing more than 15m hours of lesson time.
School staff told the Guardian that learning was almost impossible as temperature records were broken, with pupil behaviour and attention deteriorating rapidly.

One primary school teacher said: “Everyone was lying or sitting on the floor with their water bottles, sweating, moaning and feeling tired, [complaining of] headaches and nausea. The adults barely coped and most of the children were calling for their mummies and daddies. There was no learning, just surviving the best we could.”

This summer’s severe heat was not confined to the UK: brutal temperatures and devastating wildfires hit countries across Europe. One of the key demands of the student protesters that have taken to the streets in France this week has been action to make classrooms bearable during extreme heat.

Kebede warned that in the UK the impact of these bouts of extreme weather was falling hardest on more disadvantaged communities. He said children were often being sent home to flats that were unsuited to extreme heat, and to parents and carers who were unable to work from home or take time off.

“It is having a really uneven impact and it’s particularly impacting children who live in deprived urban areas … you will have a two-tier system where schools in more affluent areas are able to cope with extreme heat.”

Kebede said many of the UK’s schools were housed in either old Victorian-era buildings or those built in the 1960s and 1970s, and neither style was equipped to cope with the extreme heat that is expected to become a feature of UK summers.

He said a major capital building programme could transform schools, making them “fit for the century we are living in” and also creating good unionised apprenticeships and jobs, revitalising local communities.
“We really need plans in place now because [what we experienced this summer] is going to be the norm,” Kebede said.

articles.title: Capital punishment is surging in the US – but after Christa Pike’s botched execution, what is its future?
articles.summary:
Trump has used the full might of the presidency to supercharge executions, but an avalanche of mishaps has put the system’s flaws in the spotlight

It took more than an hour to establish the…

blocks.text: It took more than an hour to establish the two intravenous lines through which Christa Pike would be injected with a giant and normally lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital, and in that time she did everything she could to assist those who were attempting to kill her.

“Please try here,” she said over and over again to Tennessee’s execution team, pointing to specific parts of her body where she thought they might find a vein as they repeatedly stabbed her with needles. “Please try here, I think it will be OK. Please try up on my shoulder, higher.”

When the team finally achieved what they thought would be a working line, allowing her execution to proceed, Pike, 50, made a point of thanking them. “Miss Pike was kind, and she was cooperative,” her lawyer Randy Spivey, a witness in the death chamber, said.
The world knows what happened next. For reasons as yet not fully understood, the drug did not enter her bloodstream, probably spilling into her arm tissue.

blocks.caption: Media witnesses leave Riverbend maximum security institution after the execution of Christa Pike was halted in Nashville on 30 September.  Photograph: George Walker IV/AP

blocks.text: Pike, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder when she was 18 of her classmate Colleen Slemmer, remained alive. She is the only person ever to survive a full “lethal” injection execution.
On Tuesday she remarkably regained consciousness. She is now able to talk and walk around the room, her lawyers have said.
In comments to reporters, Spivey said that he was haunted by the harrowing failed execution. “What I saw is not something that should ever happen again. It was done in all of our names.”

The events of the past 10 days – starting with Pike amicably assisting her executioners and ending with her waking up shackled to a Nashville hospital bed, her arms grotesquely swollen, facing a long and uncertain road to recovery – has thrown America into a frenzy. If this is the outcome of a punishment carried out in “all our names”, then what are we doing about it?

“This is a very big moment,” said Laura Porter, executive director at the US Campaign to End the Death Penalty, an alliance of 60 abolitionist groups. “When you see something as horrific as this, the impact is enormous, as it throws attention on the death penalty’s flaws.”

Porter has been closely involved in America’s struggle with capital punishment for almost a quarter century, since she became a leader of New Yorkers Against the Death Penalty in 2003. At that time death row prisoners were still being killed at a rate of more than one a week.

There were 71 executions that year in the US (down from the 1999 pinnacle of 98). Since then, Porter has watched and agitated as the number has steadily declined for almost two decades, reaching a low of just 11 judicial killings in 2021.

“I believe that the death penalty will die by a thousand cuts,” she said. “Every time there’s a botched execution like Christa’s, or a wrongful conviction, or the execution of an intellectually disabled person, public understanding of the system’s flaws grows.”

blocks.caption: Christa Pike’s attorneys Randy Spivey, center, and Luke Ihnen, right, hold a news conference in Nashville on 7 October.  Photograph: George Walker IV/AP

blocks.text: How great a difference a few years can make. Six years ago, there was such confidence in the historic fading away of the practice that the authoritative Death Penalty Information Center (DPI) began its yearly report with the words: “Capital punishment continued to wither across the US in 2019”.

But as Mark Twain might have put it, reports of the death penalty’s own death turned out to be an exaggeration. Fast forward to last year, and DPI was recording that the 47 executions carried out in 2025 marked the highest incidence in 16 years.

No awards for guessing the key individual behind the resurgence. Less than a year after DPI’s “withering” pronouncement, Donald Trump embarked on one of the most concentrated bursts of US state killing of its own citizens in modern times.

Toward the end of his first presidency, the Trump administration executed 13 federal death row prisoners. They included Lisa Montgomery, a woman with such a shocking history of childhood sexual abuse it bears comparison to Pike’s own.

Since his return to the White House last year, Trump has used the full might of the presidency to supercharge executions. On his first day back he issued an executive order on “restoring the death penalty” in which he said it was “an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes”.

The statement was a classic Trump fabrication. The US justice department itself has concluded that there is no proof that the punishment deters criminals. Many prisoners on death row cannot be described as the most heinous, not least the 4% who by conservative estimations are innocent.

At federal level, Trump has been hampered by Joe Biden, who before he left office commuted the death penalties of all but three prisoners on federal death row. Using his power as commander-in-chef, Trump still managed this week to order the military execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, the 2009 Fort Hood mass shooter.

On Thursday the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, breathlessly announced that Hasan would face a firing squad of soldiers at Fort Hood on 3 December in the first public execution to be staged in the US since 1936. “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”

The Pentagon’s plan to livestream Hasan’s execution prompted a second wave of desbelief that ricocheted around the globe , threatening to drown out even the consternation over Pike’s treatment. US politicians denounced the idea as “disgusting”, while the UN issued the US government with the same stern warning it has given Afghanistan and Iran that the move would be tantamount to torture.

When not presiding over an administration that seems determined to turn the clock back 100 years, Trump has also used his squawk box to exhort death penalty states, where most capital punishment activity occurs, to hit the gas. Many have obliged.
First among them has been Florida. The outgoing governor, Ron DeSantis, appears to have been so inspired by Trump’s 2020-21 killing spree that he greenlit a record 19 executions last year.

DeSantis will come close to matching that shattering number in 2026. Florida has already put to death 16 prisoners this year, with two more executions pending, though the governor cancelled a lethal injection procedure on Friday without giving an explanation.

Nationwide, the US is set to kill up to 38 people this year – the most recent just on Wednesday when Texas executed convicted murderer Jamaal Howard. That tally would be down from last year’s high, but still represent a larger display of state killing than in any year since 2013.

In cheerleading the revival of executions, Trump has been backed by a supporting cast of Christian nationalists. These Bible thumpers have injected their eye-for-an-eye brand of retributive justice into the wider Maga movement.

Brooklyn Walker, an assistant professor at the University of Tennessee Knoxville, has studied Christian nationalist views on justice. She has found them to be far more embracing of retribution, including the death sentence, than other US religious groups.
Christian nationalist leaders frequently invoke Old Testament notions of punitive justice “as part of the idea of creating a social order, and then requiring people to fit within it,” Walker said.

Doug Wilson, an Idaho pastor who wants to turn America into a theocracy and has close ties to Hegseth, has pushed for legal appeals to be streamlined. That way death row prisoners could be dispatched more quickly.

Joel Webbon, another leading Christian nationalist pastor from Texas, has argued for the death penalty to be expanded to include women who make false sexual assault accusations. The day after Pike’s failed execution he posted to his 120,000 followers on X that “you cannot be pro life without being pro death penalty”.

blocks.caption: Leslie Brown, right, stands with others in the area reserved for people in favor to the death penalty outside Riverbend maximum security institution before the planned execution of Christa Pike. Photograph: George Walker IV/AP

blocks.text: The energy blown into capital punishment from such far-right religious pundits is affecting the furious debate that has now erupted in Tennessee over what should happen to Pike. Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate for Tennessee governor, wants to plug back in the electric chair.

Blackburn’s call for the return of “Old Sparky” speaks volumes about the state of capital punishment. The horrifying scenes at Pike’s attempted execution were part of a wider unravelling of lethal injections, the protocol that has been dominant in the US for almost 50 years.

By DPI’s calculations, there have been 12 botched executions in the past five years alone. Five of the condemned prisoners involved, including Pike herself, survived the procedure meaning that they were rendered immobile while a team of masked strangers failed to kill them for up to several hours.

Amid such unconscionable suffering, the claim made on behalf of lethal injections that they are a medicalised and humane form of ending a life has come unstuck. Who would dare to classify what Pike endured as humane?

Proponents of the ultimate punishment have been forced to seek alternatives that might avoid some of the pitfalls of lethal injections. But the moment they have introduced such often archaic methods they have run into a whole new set of headaches.

Two of the prisoners who survived recent lethal injections, Alan Miller and Kenneth Smith, were executed by Alabama a year later under the experimental technique, nitrogen gas. The method is regarded by veterinarians as too cruel for the euthanisia of cats and dogs, and it has now been blocked for human use by a federal court.

Other states have tried the firing squad. But when South Carolina took this path last year with Mikal Mahdi, a convicted murderer, the marksmen missed the target of the prisoner’s heart, causing him a prolonged and likely agonising death.

Such an avalanche of mishaps, spanning botched executions, experimentation, and even dark insinuations of deliberate miss-targeting, is what Porter means by her “death by a thousand cuts”. It gives her and her army of abolitionists the material they need to sustain a long campaign.

As a seasoned abolitionist, Porter knows that she is facing tough adversaries in Trump and the Christian nationalists. But she draws sustenance from the 23 states that have scrapped the death penalty which, if you add the four states that have put the practice on hold, pushes them into the majority.

Then there is the growing number of young Americans who no longer support the punishment. In the most recent Gallup poll that asked the question, from 2024, only 42% of 18 to 34 year olds approved. (In last year’s poll the overall extent of support had fallen from a 1995 high of 80% to 52%).
She also takes heart from the burgeoning ranks of Republican state lawmakers willing to raise objections. And by the increasing unwillingness of juries to mete out new death sentences.

Most of all, she’s buoyed up by the powerful accord she has found from an unlikely source: families of capital murder victims. Amid their grief, some families have had the strength and conviction to join the fight to spare the lives of those who killed their loved ones.
“In every campaign I’ve been part of where we’ve ended the death penalty – in Connecticut, Maryland, Virginia, and many more – victims’ families have been among the lead voices,” Porter said.

To those voices we may perhaps, in time, be able to add one more. It would be the most unlikely voice of all – that of a woman whom the modern state, with all its paraphernalia, could not silence: Christa Pike.

blocks.caption: Shannon Howard and Ingrid McIntyre hug outside Riverbend maximum security institution on 30 September. Photograph: George Walker IV/AP

blocks.text: Her lawyers tell us that she is angry and confused, her mind foggy. But she is also able to inquire after the well-being of others, including, poignantly, the family of her victim, Colleen Slemmer.

She is not out of the woods: on Saturday she was released from hospital and returned to the women’s prison in Nashville, where she will still receive medical care. But coming from a state of unconsciousness so profound that even her own legal team feared she might be brain-dead, her reemergence has been nothing short of astonishing.
It all leaves so many questions, her lawyer Spivey said ruefully on Wednesday. “We have to ask, ‘How much suffering is enough?’”
Spivey directed the question at Tennessee. He might just as well have been addressing America.

articles.title: Reinhard Jumamoy’s audacity, work ethic give NU its go-to guy
articles.summary: In Reinhard Jumamoy, the NU Bulldogs have found the brazen leader they need

blocks.text: GAME HERO. NU’s Reinhard Jumamoy comes through for the Bulldogs against the UST Growling Tigers in the UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball tournament.
UAAP
In Reinhard Jumamoy, the NU Bulldogs have found the brazen leader they need

items: Reinhard Jumamoy hit a crucial three-pointer in the final seconds to secure a victory for NU against UST, finishing the game with 16 points.
Despite struggling with his shooting earlier in the game, Jumamoy demonstrated confidence and leadership, taking the decisive shot when it mattered most.
NU's win improved their record to 4-2, keeping them in the top three of the UAAP Season 89 men's basketball standings.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – NU was on the verge of blowing a 15-point lead against UST, and the Bulldogs needed someone to take charge.

Macmac Alfanta hit a fourth-quarter triple, Mo Diassana came through with lobs and putbacks inside, and Paul Francisco drained a crucial short stab in the final two minutes of overtime. But when the game came down to its final possession, it was Reinhard Jumamoy who delivered the decisive blow.

With NU down 84-85 with five seconds left, Jumamoy, fresh off getting blocked by UST big man Collins Akowe on the previous possession, launched a contested triple that banked in to lift the Bulldogs to an 87-85 victory.
For Jumamoy, the game-winner was proof of his audacity and self-belief, trusting his work ethic to deliver despite taking a contested three-pointer with NU down by just one.

“I just told myself that I was going to take the shot. I practice that, after all. Coach always tells me that I have a lot of kapal ng mukha (brazenness), so I just took charge,” Jumamoy said in Filipino after the game.
“I guess when I went for the layup against Collins, I remembered what happened to us last year when I turned the ball over. So I told myself I had to take charge and lead my teammates,” he added.
Jumamoy finished with a team-high 16 points, 6 rebounds and 6 assists, shooting 7-of-16 from the field and 4-of-13 from beyond the arc.
The game-winner was especially gutsy considering he had missed his previous five three-point attempts. But the misses did little to take away his confidence when NU needed him most.
“I have nothing to say, really. I just told myself I was going to take the shot because I practice that,” Jumamoy said. “Win or lose. By God’s grace, my shot went in.”
The victory improved NU’s record to 4-2, keeping the Bulldogs in the top three of the UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball standings.

Francisco, who made the pass to Jumamoy in the final play, had no hesitation trusting Jumamoy with the game on the line, especially after his point guard told him he wanted the ball before the inbound play.

“Before the inbound play, Reinhard came up to me and said, ‘If nothing’s there, just give it to me.’ So I trusted my point guard. There weren’t any other options because UST played good denial defense on our play. I saw Reinhard, so I trusted him with the pass,” Francisco said.
NU head coach Jeff Napa, who has mentored Jumamoy since his days with the NU-Nazareth School high school program, knew his starting guard had the confidence to take and make a shot of that magnitude.
Napa believed Jumamoy was the player most willing to shoulder the responsibility even with the outcome hanging in the balance.
“I’ll give Reinhard credit for the game-winner. That was his shot to take. Win or lose, he took it and made it, and things went our way,” Napa said in Filipino.

“But under pressure, that’s when you really test a player’s character and see how willing they are to push themselves. Despite what happened in the third and fourth quarters, when we became too complacent, at least we got to see that character,” Napa said.
The Bulldogs will end the first round against league-leading FEU Tamaraws next Sunday, October 18, at the Blue Eagle Gym. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Not an endorsement of genocide: Pangilinan, LP defend Leni Robredo meeting with Israeli envoy
articles.summary: Senator Kiko Pangilinan and the Liberal Party of the Philippines (LP) defended Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo over her meeting with Israeli Ambassador Dana Kursh, saying that receiving a city guest…

blocks.text: Published October 11, 2026 12:38pm

Senator Kiko Pangilinan and the Liberal Party of the Philippines (LP) defended Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo over her meeting with Israeli Ambassador Dana Kursh, saying that receiving a city guest does not mean an endorsement of genocide.
“Public officials have diplomatic responsibilities. Fulfilling these responsibilities doesn't mean they support the atrocities being committed,” Pangilinan said in a statement on Saturday.
“We continue to stand for the protection of human rights, especially of civilians, and accountability, including under international law,” he added.
Pangilinan was Robredo’s running mate during the 2022 presidential elections.
The LP echoed the senator’s sentiments, saying the public should be fair when making judgments.

“Walang naipakitang ebidensiya na sa pagtanggap sa embahador ay nagpahayag si Mayor Robredo ng pagsang-ayon sa mga operasyong militar ng Israel sa Gaza. Magkaiba ang pakikipag-ugnayang diplomatiko at pagsuporta sa mga patakaran ng isang pamahalaan,” the party said in a separate statement on Saturday.

(No evidence was presented that Mayor Robredo expressed support for Israel’s military operations in Gaza by receiving the ambassador. Diplomatic engagement is different from supporting a government’s policies.)
Robredo, a former vice president, welcomed Kursh during her courtesy visit at Naga City Hall on Oct. 5, 2026, which is part of the latter’s visit to the Bicol region.
The LP added it recognizes the public’s right to ask questions, criticize, and hold government officials accountable.

“Ngunit kaakibat ng karapatang ito ang responsibilidad na maging patas at tapat sa katotohanan. Sa mga usaping may kinalaman sa karapatang pantao, mahalagang maging malinaw ang ating mga prinsipyo at maingat sa ating mga paghatol,” the party said.
(However, this right comes with the responsibility to be fair and truthful. On issues involving human rights, it is important to be clear about our principles and careful in our judgments.)

The LP reiterated its stance on human rights, the safety of civilians, and accountability for violations of international law, which includes the rights of Palestinians to security, dignity, and self-determination.
On October 7, 2023, Hamas militants attacked Israel, prompting a military offensive by Israel in Gaza that killed and displaced thousands of Palestinians.
On the 2026 anniversary of the attack, Israel stepped up its air and ground offensive in Gaza with more attacks on Hamas militants and command posts on Monday.

For its part, Hamas said it struck Israel's commercial capital Tel Aviv with a missile salvo, setting off sirens in central Israel. Two people were lightly wounded, according to the Israeli ambulance service.

The Philippines has expressed its support for a two-state solution to resolve the Palestinian and Israeli conflict and stressed that it stands in solidarity with Palestine in their goal to achieve peace and prosperity.

"The Philippines’ support for the two-state solution has never wavered, and we firmly believe that genuine and enduring peace would not prevail in the Middle East without the establishment of an independent and viable Palestinian State,” said then Foreign Affairs Undersecretary for Migration Affairs Leo Herrera-Lim.—RF, GMA News

articles.title: US: Justice Department probes Trump's press pool boycott for antitrust violation
articles.summary: The Department of Justice is investigating whether the five news organizations violated antitrust laws when they suspended their coverage of Trump in protest. The networks under probe are ABC, CBS,…

image.caption: Trump has long been at odds with the mainstream media, regularly calling them 'fake news' [FILE: September 2026]Image: Alex Wroblewski/AFP

blocks.text: The US Department of Justice announced on Saturday that it is investigating whether the White House press pool's decision to halt coverage of President Donald Trump last month, violated the nation's anti trust law.
Group boycotts among business competitors might violate US law, spokesperson Emily Covington said.
"The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws," she said.
The networks under the scrutiny are ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News.
Jose Zamora, the Committee to Protect Journalists' regional director of the Americas, criticized the administration's decision to investigate.
"The government should not use antitrust investigations to intimidate news outlets defending press access," Zamora said on X. "The public's right to know depends on that access."
Under pressure — Trump's fractured America
Why is Trump's press pool under investigation?

On September 21, a pool of five broadcasters ceased presidential coverage after the Trump administration barred news networks CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, saying covering the president was a "privilege, not a right."
Trump bans media outlets from White House
As a result, the five television networks suspended coverage in protest and refused to provide replacement program.

The news outlets also sued the administration, accusing it of violating free speech and free press rights under the First Amendment of the US Constitution and pursuing retaliation over their coverage.
On September 24, the White House reinstated their press credentials after a US district Judge ordered the administration to "immediately return, reinstate and restore" their access.
The president has repeatedly called the mainstream media "fake news" and clashed with reporters during interviews.
The White House press pool is a roating group of news outlets which cover the president and accompany him on official duties.

CNN is one of the five news organizations, along with ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBS, that make up the primary White House television pool. They share the cost of covering the president and take turns organizing coverage and share the footage with outlets around the country.
The White House press pool has now become a proxy for a fight over press freedom.

articles.title: Chinese militia vessel, 22 sampans intrude into Palawan waters
articles.summary: The National Task Force for the West Philippine Sea condemned the intrusion of a Chinese maritime militia vessel and 22 sampans into Kota Island’s territorial sea in Palawan, where the vessels…

blocks.text: October 11, 2026 | 11:16am
The Philippine Coast Guard drives away a Chinese maritime militia vessel and 22 fishing boats from the territorial waters of Kota Island in Palawan on Oct. 9, 2026.
Jay Tarriela via Facebook / Philstar.com's screenshot

MANILA, Philippines — The National Task Force for the West Philippine Sea (NTF-WPS) condemned the intrusion of a Chinese maritime militia vessel and 22 sampans into Kota Island’s territorial sea in Palawan, where the vessels allegedly engaged in unauthorized fishing and dumped waste at sea.

In a statement released on Saturday, October 10, the NTF-WPS said Chinese Maritime Militia Vessel 9622 deployed the 22 sampans near the island on October 9. One of the sampans approached as close as 250 meters from the shoreline.

“When Philippine Coast Guard personnel, supported by the Philippine Marine Corps and the Philippine Navy, moved to address the intrusion, the Chinese mothership maneuvered around and encircled their boats, while its master brazenly claimed the area as Chinese territory and directed the Philippine team to leave,” the task force said.
The NTF-WPS said the Philippine personnel’s response led to the departure of all Chinese vessels from the island’s territorial sea.
Kota Island is part of the Municipality of Kalayaan in Palawan, and its territorial sea is under Philippine sovereignty, the task force said.

“The Chinese vessels’ unauthorized fishing activities violate Philippine laws, including Republic Act No. 12064 (Philippine Maritime Zones Act) and Republic Act No. 8550 (Philippine Fisheries Code), as amended by RA No. 10654,” the NTF-WPS said.
“China’s claim over the area has no basis under international law,” it added.
The task force said the incident involved the same Chinese maritime militia vessel that deployed 24 sampans near the island on September 28.
“Such repeated incursions underscore the need for sustained vigilance and a clear, consistent response to attempts to challenge Philippine sovereignty,” the NTF-WPS said.
The task force commended the Philippine Coast Guard, Philippine Marine Corps and Philippine Navy for their “firm, coordinated, and professional response.”
It said it would continue supporting the Coast Guard and other concerned agencies in protecting Philippine territory and maritime rights.
“Repeated intrusions, coercive maneuvers, and baseless assertions of sovereignty will not be allowed to become normalized in Philippine waters,” the NTF-WPS said.
“The Philippines will continue to respond firmly, lawfully, and resolutely to protect its sovereignty, territorial integrity, and national interests in the West Philippine Sea,” it added.

articles.title: Williams, Ramirez lead Guardians past White Sox in Game 5 to cap ALDS comeback
articles.summary: Gavin Williams struck out 12, Jose Ramirez homered on a pitch just above home plate and the Cleveland Guardians beat the Chicago White Sox 2-0 Saturday night to complete a comeback from an 0-2…

(Sue Ogrocki/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: MLB·Recap

Gavin Williams struck out 12, Jose Ramirez homered on a pitch just above home plate and the Cleveland Guardians beat the Chicago White Sox 2-0 Saturday night to complete a comeback from an 0-2 deficit in their best-of-five AL Division Series.
Cleveland overcame 0-2 deficit in best-of-5-series, hasn't won World Series since 1948

Gavin Williams struck out 12, José Ramirez homered on a pitch just above home plate and the Cleveland Guardians beat the Chicago White Sox 2-0 Saturday night to complete a comeback from an 0-2 deficit in their best-of-five AL Division Series.

Cleveland opens the AL Championship Series at Tampa Bay on Monday night, seeking its first World Series trip since 2016. The Guardians franchise hasn't won the title since 1948, the longest drought among MLB teams.
Guardians pitchers struck out 21, the most in a nine-inning post-season game. The White Sox got just three hits, put only nine balls in play and struck out 75 times over the series.
CLEVELAND ROCKS! https://t.co/CCRZQnb7yG—MLB
Two days after saving Game 4, Williams became just the third pitcher in post-season history to get the last out of a game and start the following game when his team faced elimination in both.

He didn't allow a hit until Kyle Teel looped a knuckle-curve into right field with two outs in the sixth, two innings after Ramirez homered for the second straight game, a two-run drive off Sean Burke.
After a walk loaded the bases, Erik Sabrowski of Edmonton relieved and struck out Munetaka Murakami on a foul tip, the pitcher letting out a yell.
Williams's 12 strikeouts tied Cleveland's record for a post-season game. He got 22 swings and misses, and his 24 strikeouts over three games tied for second-most in a best-of-five post-season series.
Canada's Smith records 5-out save

Hunter Gaddis followed Sabrowski and got four outs, and Cade Smith of Abbotsford, B.C., finished for his first career five-out save, striking out the side in the ninth. He blew a fastball by Tristan Peters of Winkler, Man., for the final out, setting off a celebration at Cleveland's Progressive Field.
The Guardians erase an 0-2 series deficit and advance to the ALCS! #CLINCHED (MLB x @BudweiserUSA) https://t.co/g0zCsmeMPB—MLB
Chicago, the first team to reach the playoffs after three straight 100-loss seasons, has not won the World Series since 2004.

Ramirez homered on a knuckle-curve 0.74 feet above ground, the lowest pitch hit for a post-season home run since tracking started in 2008, according to MLB Statcast, and the lowest hit by Ramirez in his 14-year big league career.
Steven Kwan had singled leading off the fourth ahead of Ramirez's sixth post-season homer, which went just over the wall near the right-field line.
Murakami and Andrew Benintendi struck out four times each, and Teel and Chase Meidroth three times apiece.
Up next

Tampa Bay went 5-1 against the Guardians, including a three-game sweep at Tropicana Field in July. It will be the third post-season meeting of the teams following the Rays' win in the 2013 wild card game and the Guardians' sweep in the 2022 Wild Card Series.

articles.title: [Two Pronged] I left my husband over his secret cross-dressing — and took the blame for the breakup
articles.summary: Our letter sender endured seven broken promises before finally walking out on her husband's secret cross-dressing. But now, she faces a new dilemma: is it time to tell her family and friends the…

blocks.text: Rappler’s People section runs an advice column by couple Jeremy Baer and clinical psychologist Dr. Margarita Holmes.

Jeremy has a master’s degree in law from Oxford University. A banker of 37 years who worked in three continents, he has been training with Dr. Holmes for the last 10 years as co-lecturer and, occasionally, as co-therapist, especially with clients whose financial concerns intrude into their daily lives.
Together, they have written two books: Love Triangles: Understanding the Macho-Mistress Mentality and Imported Love: Filipino-Foreign Liaisons.
Dear Dr. Holmes and Mr. Baer:
I was married to my husband for 20 years. We have 2 children together, both girls. Both girls have also graduated with AB degrees and both want to be lawyers like my husband is.

He is a very good provider. I also work as a professional, but I realize I would not be able to work part time the way I do if I were not married to him. I would have to work full time to support myself.
There is no other man in my life, so you might wonder why I left him. Many of my friends wonder — including my own parents and siblings, which hurt the most.
I have not told them he is a cross-dresser, though I am sure enough people know that it will be common knowledge in time.

People like to gossip about fallen heroes and that is what will happen to him — ESPECIALLY to someone like him, who is very successful, has a reputation that makes him well known even internationally.

I finally gave up on the 21st year of our marriage. It was the seventh time he promised he would stop cross-dressing and failed. It used to hurt me the first three times it happened. We went to counseling so many times. I could not accept his behavior and he could not stop it.

I loved him so much and could not understand why he would continue to do this, despite the fact that it hurt our marriage. Then I fell out of love with him. Can you imagine making love to someone who wore more makeup than you?
When I finally left, the children understood but he did not. He started to bad-mouth me, without sharing what really broke the camel’s back. I kept quiet through all his lies and persecution.

It is now three years since I left him, and he repeatedly asks me to get back together with him, promising he has changed. But I see his social media, hear stories from his so-called friends and know he hasn’t changed at all.
What should I do?
Emma
Dear Emma,
Thank you for your email.

If I understand correctly, you left your husband because of his cross-dressing and his broken promises to stop. You then chose not to reveal that this was why you left him, which resulted in your family (other than your children) and friends not understanding why you brought your marriage to an end. Your question now is: What should I do?
It seems that while your husband’s cross-dressing was an issue, the fundamental reason your relationship broke down was the pattern of broken promises.

Marriage is not easy at the best of times and a constant stream of hopes and expectations being dashed is likely to undermine anyone’s faith in its continuance. Your decision to leave was entirely reasonable and the answer to your question is that you should remain resolute in that decision. There is, after all, no sign that the leopard has changed his spots.

The matter of who you tell about the reasons for your decision is something else. You imply that your husband’s fondness for cross-dressing features in his social media postings and it is therefore reasonable to suppose it is now quite widely known among those who have access to those postings. This surely should ease the burden that you have taken on, namely to leave him but not explain why, thus opening yourself to criticism that you have deliberately allowed to remain unanswered.

Perhaps it is time to change your tune and tell the truth, at least to a limited number of those with whom you have close relationships. This will finally enable them to understand why you acted as you did and will no doubt lead to some relief from adverse comment on your part as well as counteract any further lies and persecution on his part.
With best wishes,
-JAF Baer
Dear Emma:

Thank you very much for your letter. I agree with Mr .Baer’s response and I also agree with your not telling anyone else the reasons you left your husband. To do so would just be to open a can of worms with everybody who knew, probably telling “just this one person” despite having been sworn to secrecy. Then you would have everyone and his uncle share their opinion (educated or otherwise) with you. God, what a bore! Not to mention kakainis (pissy off-ie).

I also understand why you would be hurt about your parents and your siblings not understanding why you left the marriage. I think that perhaps the issue was not so much not “understanding” since there are many things we do that others do not — or refuse to — understand. It is as though they have forgotten you are a caring yet logical person, and you would have your own (good) reasons for doing so.
An example might be your husband’s not “understanding” how much his being a cross-dresser and all that went with it would change your viewing him as the same man you married.

Yes, yes, we all know that cross-dressing does not mean you are transgender or gay. It is also easy being objective about data you read about the concept of cross-dressing or even about loving someone close to you who cross-dresses.

But the specific dynamics of your marriage makes/made it difficult for you to accept the way he cross-dressed. It seems he accepted this, thus his constant promises to stop doing it, and yet he seemed unable to do so.
SO…what are you to do? I would think go on as you have been: be a good person, gentle with others, including your children, your ex-husband, the rest of your family, your friends, and yourself.
All the very best,
– MG Holmes
Life got complicated? Write to our Two Pronged duo at twopronged@rappler.com.

articles.title: ‘My body is still peaking’: Eliud Kipchoge wins first marathon in three years
articles.summary:
• Kenyan breaks Melbourne Marathon record by two seconds

  • ‘I’m happy to run with the gen Zs,’ 41-year-old says

Marathon’s greatest competitor, Eliud Kipchoge,…

blocks.text: Marathon’s greatest competitor, Eliud Kipchoge, has sent a message to the next generation declaring that he’s not done yet.
The 41-year-old Kenyan revelled in his Melbourne Marathon debut on Sunday, breaking the race record and delighting thousands of fans at the MCG finish.
Beating the old race mark by two seconds, his two hours nine minutes and 10 seconds over a new course gave Kipchoge his first marathon win in three years.

Jimmy Whelan, a former Australian professional cyclist, was with the two-time Olympic champion and former world record-holder until about 30km. Then Kipchoge went up a gear and dominated to the finish.
Looking as though he has just done a training run, Kipchoge then spent well over half an hour celebrating with fans along the MCG boundary fence.
He was mobbed by media at the finish and took the chaos in his stride.
“The crowd is so wonderful – I’ve never seen a crowd like this,” he said. “Melbourne is really, really a sporting city.
“I believe that my body is still peaking – still able to compete with the next generation. The oldest athlete is still competing but I am happy to run with the gen Zs.”
“I [increased] the pace after 30km, to see whether I can run well and beat the [race record]. My plan went well.”

Kipchoge had said repeatedly over the last few days that his Melbourne visit was more than just another race. It is the third leg in his world tour, where he will run a marathon on each continent, including Antarctica.

blocks.caption: Kipchoge celebrates with fans at the MCG.  Photograph: Ye Myo Khant/Sopa Images/Shutterstock

blocks.text: He has also done some community work while in Melbourne and is acutely aware of the city’s rich sporting heritage.
“The experience is awesome – the culture of Melbourne is wonderful,” he said.
“The last four days, I’ve seen myself, sport can do wonder. It was four-in-one – with the tennis, finishing at the cricket, the Olympics were here in 1956, running on the Formula One track.
after newsletter promotion
“I will come back to Melbourne to watch the tennis, the Formula One next year, to see people of Melbourne playing cricket. This is the best track ever.”
Kipchoge could have finished a few seconds quicker but was waving to the crowd on the half-lap inside the MCG to the finish.
This is his second visit to Australia. The Kenyan finished ninth in the 2025 Sydney Marathon.
Australia’s Thomas Do Canto was runner-up in 2:10:35 and Whelan was fifth. New Zealand’s Camille French won the women’s race in 2:28:25, with Australia’s Sinead Diver next in 2:28.49.
The Australian Seth O’Donnell and the New Zealander Georgie Gregec won the half-marathon titles.
Earlier on Sunday, a woman was taken to hospital after she was struck by a car near Flinders Street station, about 200 metres from the marathon route.
Reports suggest police officers in the vicinity drew their weapons after the car, which was seen driving erratically, hit the woman about 10.45am, before performing a U-turn and driving away.
The woman was taken to Royal Melbourne hospital and her condition is not known.

The Philippine STAR / Miguel de Guzman
MANILA, Philippines — The Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) may bring rain to Southern Luzon, parts of the Visayas and Mindanao, PAGASA said.

In its weather forecast on Sunday, October 11, PAGASA said that Mindanao, Bicol Region, MIMAROPA, Western Visayas and Negros Island Region may expect cloudy skies with scattered rains and thunderstorms due to the ITCZ.
The rest of Visayas may also expect partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rain showers or thunderstorms due to the ITCZ.
PAGASA warned residents of these areas of possible flash floods or landslides due to moderate to at times heavy rains.
Meanwhile, Metro Manila, CALABARZON, the rest of Cagayan Valley, Aurora, Nueva Ecija and Bulacan may expect cloudy skies with scattered rains and thunderstorms due to the easterlies.
Batanes may also expect cloudy skies with rain due to the northeasterly wind flow.
The rest of Luzon may expect partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rain showers or thunderstorms due to localized thunderstorms.
Weather systems outside PAR
Two weather systems are currently outside the Philippine area of responsibility.
As of 3 a.m., Typhoon Koguma and a tropical depression are currently located east of the country.
Typhoon Koguma is estimated to be 2,795 kilometers east-northeast of extreme northern Luzon.
It has maximum sustained winds of up to 175 kilometers per hour (kph) near the center, with gusts up to 215 kph and is moving northwestward at 20 kph.
Meanwhile, a tropical depression is estimated to be 2,940 kilometers east of Southern Luzon.

articles.title: Remembering Tatay Elmer Cordero, whose happy place was protests
articles.summary: On the ground at rallies, fellow activists always looked forward to seeing longtime jeepney driver Tatay Elmer dance, waving the PISTON flag around in the air

items: Elmer Cordero, affectionately known as 'Tatay Elmer,' was a dedicated jeepney driver and activist who spent his life advocating for the transportation sector and supporting his community.
He was a loving husband to Elvie and a father figure to his niece Jamaica, whom he raised as his own, demonstrating his nurturing nature and commitment to family.
Despite health challenges, Tatay Elmer remained actively involved in protests and rallies, becoming a symbol of resilience and solidarity within the Filipino community until his passing.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Elmer Cordero was the epitome of love in its most radical form.

Much of the late activist’s life had been spent behind the wheel of his jeepney — driving passengers around on his route of MCU Rotonda-Divisoria, or sometimes, Malanday-Divisioria. He would bring home between P400 to P500 on good days.
When he wasn’t driving, he was out rallying on the streets with his fellow drivers at Pagkakaisa ng mga Samahan ng Tsuper at Opereytor Nationwide (PISTON).
Known as “Tatay Elmer” or “Ka Elmer” to most, the 78-year-old had spent his last waking moments doing what he loved most: protesting for the transportation sector.

PISTON president Mody Floranda shared that Tatay Elmer was at a rally on September 29 when he began to have difficulty breathing. Being the strong old man that he was, he even managed to walk himself to the terminal to catch a ride to a hospital in Caloocan City, where he would be confined for several days before eventually succumbing to the complications brought about by his heart attack.

blocks.caption: REST IN PEACE. Tatay Elmer’s casket is adorned with placards and the PISTON flag. Juno Reyes/Rappler

blocks.text: Floranda’s anecdote alone already says a lot about who Tatay Elmer was as a person — someone who was pro-people until the very end.
But Tatay Elmer was many other things to the people around him.

He met his wife, Elvie, when she worked as his secretary at the repair shop he was running in Fairview. Right off the bat, she liked that he was kind and easygoing, and this was something that would manifest throughout their marriage.
As a husband, he became a master of the art of pagsusuyo, and Elvie — who admitted that she sometimes had a sharp tongue — was always willing to be swayed by Tatay Elmer.

“Hindi naman maiiwasan sa mag-asawa ‘yung magtatalo. Nagtatalo-talo kami (As husband and wife, we couldn’t avoid the occasional argument),” she told Rappler as she sat on the first pew of the Resurrection Chapel at Claret Church, where his wake is being held.

blocks.caption: Tatay Elmer’s wife, Elvie, sits in front of his casket at his wake in Quezon City. Juno Reyes/Rappler

blocks.text: Still, they were always quick to make up in the end, and would never go long without patching things up.
“Kahit kasalanan ko, siya unang sumusuyo. Mas marami akong kasalanan. Hindi ‘yan aalis nang hindi kami nagbabati,” the widow added with a slight chuckle.
(Even when it was my fault, he would always be the first to appease me. I had more faults. He wouldn’t leave the house until we were okay.)

The two never had kids of their own. But for the past nine years, they had been raising little Jamaica since she was a baby. While she is the child of Elvie’s nephew, Tatay Elmer was adamant about caring for Jamaica, who has taken to calling the old couple “mommy” and “daddy.”
Now in the third grade, Jamaica had even served as Tatay Elmer’s occasional companion at rallies.
“Naaalala ko po, nung pumunta kami sa Manila, pinasyal niya ako. Tapos, nagmartsa kami (I remember he took me sightseeing when we went to Manila. Then, we marched in a rally),” Jamaica recounted.
Tatay Elmer had stood not just as a father to Jamaica, but also to the youths he would cross paths with at rallies.

Elvie had joked that it was a good thing these students didn’t avoid him even if he was old, to which the longtime jeepney driver and activist replied, “Hindi ah, mababait ang mga estudyante. Buti nga marami akong naging anak (No, the students are all very kind. It’s a good thing I ended up having lots of children because of them).”

Many of the students whose lives he had touched stayed at his wake all day as soon as it opened to the public. They had helped keep Jamaica entertained, and had even prepared a special performance later that night to pay tribute to Tatay Elmer.
Tatay Elmer was also never one to skimp on showing support to those around him, even if it meant putting his own health and safety at risk.

He had been confined at the hospital when Floranda set out to file his certificate of candidacy for senator in 2025. Much to the PISTON president’s surprise, Tatay Elmer appeared right in front of him at Luneta, still wearing a hospital bracelet.

blocks.caption: PISTON president Mody Floranda attends the wake of Tatay Elmer. Juno Reyes/Rappler

blocks.text: “Sabi ko, ‘Bakit narito ka? ‘Di ba nakaconfine ka sa Jose Reyes?’ Sabi niya, ‘Hindi ako papayag na hindi kita sasamahan sa Comelec,’” Floranda recalled.
(I said, “Why are you here? Aren’t you supposed to be confined at Jose Reyes?” He said, “I’m not going to allow myself to not accompany you to the Comelec.”)
Tatay Elmer had apparently evaded the hospital security guard’s watchful eye to make his stealthy escape. It might seem uncharacteristic for a sickly man in his 70s, but not for Tatay Elmer.

On the ground at rallies, fellow activists would always look forward to seeing him dance as he waved the PISTON flag around in the air. Protests were his happy place, and it was through his staunch defense of the transportation sector that he felt most alive.

blocks.caption: Tatay Elmer at the campaign rally of Leni Robredo and Kiko Pangilinan in 2022. Photo by Ryan Eduard Benaid/PonD News Asia

blocks.text: “Talagang makikita mo ‘yung saya niya ‘pag may mga rally. Hindi mo mararamdaman sa kanya ‘yung pagod (You could really see how happy he was at rallies. You could never feel that he was tired),” Floranda shared.

In 2020, he became a part of the PISTON 6 — a group of jeepney drivers who were jailed for staging a protest to call for government aid. He was 72 years old at the time of his arrest, and was the oldest in the group.
It was then that he became a modern hero not just to his fellow jeepney drivers, but to the youth, and Filipinos at large.

“Doon ko lang nakita si Ka Elmer na masigasig sa pakikipaglaban sa hanay ng transportasyon,” Dionisio “Diony” Bendoy, the vice president of NOBLUDA-PISTON, told Rappler, referring to Cordero’s brave act that led to his arrest.
(It was only then that I saw Ka Elmer’s eagerness to fight for the transportation sector.)

blocks.caption: Diony Bendoy raises his fist to honor Tatay Elmer at his wake on October 9. Juno Reyes/Rappler

blocks.text: Severino Ramos, who was also a part of the PISTON 6, was among the first to attend Tatay Elmer’s wake. They had known each other long before they had gotten detained at the same time — with Ramos now unable to remember when and where it was that they had first met.

“Kasama pa rin kita. Ikaw lang nauna. Hindi lang tatagal, baka sumunod din ako (I’m still with you. You just happened to go first. Before long, I might follow you),” Ramos quipped as he shared his final message for his longtime friend.

blocks.caption: Severino Ramos, who was among the PISTON 6 with Tatay Elmer, honors the late activist and jeepney driver at his wake on October 9. Juno Reyes/Rappler

blocks.text: Those who knew Tatay Elmer in different contexts can all attest that his life was 78 years of pure love and solidarity at the maximum level. His legacy as an activist and jeepney driver was already cemented far before his death, and will continue to hold space in the collective consciousness of the Filipino people. – Rappler.com

articles.title: NMC calls out politicians who don't stand up for Filipino fishermen facing harassment in WPS
articles.summary: The National Maritime Council (NMC) on Sunday expressed its frustration over local politicians who refuse to make a stand against the repeated harassment by China on Filipino fishermen in the West…

blocks.text: Published October 11, 2026 9:54am

The National Maritime Council (NMC) on Sunday expressed its frustration over local politicians who refuse to make a stand against the repeated harassment by China on Filipino fishermen in the West Philippine Sea.

“Kung ikaw ay salungat ang sinasabi mo sa sinasabi ko, at pinapanigan mo pa yung salita ng kabila. What does it speak of us as a Filipino?” said NMC spokesperson Alexander Lopez in an interview with Super Radyo dzBB.
(If what you are saying opposes what I am saying, and you even side with the words of the other side. What does it say about us as Filipinos?)

“Tignan mo yung mga matataas na politiko, did they condemn ‘yung mga ginagawa ng Chinese government sa ating mga mangingisda sa karagatan, may narinig ba kayo? Until now, wala tayong narinig,” he added.
(Look at the high-ranking politicians, did they condemn what the Chinese government is doing to our fishermen in the sea, did you hear anything? Until now, we haven't heard anything.)
The NMC noted that Chinese vessels allegedly interfered with the medical evacuation of a Philippine Navy sailor, which delayed the transfer of the latter to a Philippine Coast Guard vessel.
“Instead na makarating sa Coast Guard vessel, na doon sana ililipat yung may sakit na tauhan natin, tumagal ng halos sampung oras na paghaharang nila,” said Lopez.
(Instead of reaching the Coast Guard vessel, where our sick personnel was supposed to be transferred, their interference that lasted for almost 10 hours. )
Also another recent incident of harassment by China was the interference on the resupply mission to Ayungin Shoal last September 24.
The NMC called on the public to make a stand amid the tensions in the West Philippine Sea.

“Iisa po ang kalaban natin dito. Pilipino tayo. Iisa ang dugo natin. Sana po ay magkaisa tayo. Let’s rally behind our flag. Ang karagatan natin ay mahalaga. Ang karagatan ay livelihood, ito ay may kinalaman sa kinabukasan,” said Lopez.

(We only have one enemy here. We are Filipinos. We share the same blood. I hope we can unite. Let’s rally behind our flag. Our seas are important. The ocean is a source of livelihood, it has to do with the future.)

In 2016, an international arbitration tribunal in The Hague ruled in favor of the Philippines over China's claims in the South China Sea, saying that it had "no legal basis." China has not recognized the decision. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Shooter kills 8 people and himself in Pennsylvania — police
articles.summary: The 45-year-old shooter, who is yet to be identified, carried out the killings at his home in Erie. Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro offered support as the lakeside city grieves.

image.caption: Law enforcement arrived at the scene early Saturday after the overnight shooting, and are continuing their investigation of the crime Image: WJET/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A man killed eight people and himself during a mass shooting at a house in Erie, Pennsylvania, local police said Saturday.
What do we know so far?

Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said seven of the eight victims were related to the shooter, with the eighth person being a family friend. The shooter had died of an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound before authorities arrived at the scene.
Among the victims was a 1-year-old girl and 5-year-old boy, with a pregnant woman also dead in the shooting.
"Some scenes stay with you long after you leave them. This is one of those tragic scenes," Lorah said, describing an "eerie silence" when police arrived at the home.

blocks.caption: The Erie SWAT team was also present at the scene of the shooting Image: Matt Barnum/WJET/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The identity of the 45-year-old shooter has not yet been revealed by authorities. The motive for the massacre is also still unclear, with police pursuing an investigation.
At a press conference, Erie Mayor Daria Devlin addressed the families of the victims.

"I am so deeply sorry. What happened to you was horrific, and there is nothing that any of us can say today that will make this any easier," she said. "But you do need to know that our entire community is with you, we're grieving with you. And we are here to support you."
Pennsylvania Governor Shapiro offers support after 'tragic mass shooting'
Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro spoke with Devlin by phone and offered his support to Erie.

"I've spoken with Mayor Devlin and offered my administration's full support following the tragic mass shooting in Erie last night — killing nine of our fellow Pennsylvanians," Shapiro said in a statement post on X.
Shapiro said his "heart breaks for this family" and added that he and his wife Lori Shapiro "are praying for their loved ones and the entire Erie community."
Shapiro, a Democrat, has pushed for gun control bills in his state and signed an executive order in 2024 to reestablish the Pennsylvania Office of Gun Violence Prevention.

articles.title: B.C. Conservative campaign director under fire for anti-Islam posts
articles.summary: The campaign director for the B.C. Conservatives is facing criticism over anti-Islam posts she shared on social media earlier this year, just days after the party fired another candidate over his own…

image.caption: Katy Merrifield, campaign director of the B.C. Conservative party, is facing criticism for anti-Islamic posts on social media. (katy_merrifield/X)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New

The campaign director for the B.C. Conservatives is facing criticism over anti-Islam posts she shared on social media earlier this year, just days after the party fired another candidate over his own offensive posts.
National Council of Canadian Muslims 'deeply hurt' by social media posts from Katy Merrifield
Campaign director Katy Merrifield posted on X in June in response to a U.K. inquiry about child sexual exploitation: "F--k Islam. Defend Western civilization." The post was later removed.

"We are deeply hurt by the comments made by B.C. Conservative Campaign Director Katy Merrifield ... [and] several subsequent posts that demonstrate a pattern of promoting Islamophobic views," the National Council of Canadian Muslims (NCCM) wrote in a post on X Friday.

A screen capture of the post on X from Katy Merrifield from June 17, accessed using the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine and blurred by CBC News. Merrifield later removed the post. (@katy_merrifield/X)

This comes after the party dropped Joachim Agou, its candidate for Victoria-Beacon Hill, over offensive social media posts targeting Palestinians and Pakistanis that came to light this week, which the council said made Merrifield's posts especially concerning.

items: B.C. Conservatives drop Victoria-Beacon Hill candidate after offensive social media posts

blocks.text: Merrifield, who previously worked as head of communications for federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, is the campaign director for the B.C. Conservative Party and not a candidate.

She acknowledged her past comments in a post Friday, saying they stemmed from her experience as a rape survivor and from feeling "heartbroken, horrified and angry" after reading accounts of sexual abuse involving young girls in the U.K. and the failure of authorities to protect them.
"I took down my original post within hours because my anger was directed at the extremism used to justify these horrific crimes, not at Muslims or their faith," Merrifield wrote.

But the NCCM said "at no point did [Merrifield] apologize for her statement or recognize the pain it caused," adding that she also did not address what it called a pattern of promoting "a range of problematic messages" on social media.
"There is no room for hate in any area of Canadian politics," the NCCM said.
Rise in Islamophobia
The NCCM said B.C. has seen a significant rise in Islamophobia, pointing to incidents involving vehicles being driven at people, attacks on imams and vandalism at mosques.

items: Police investigating threatening email sent to Muslim schools across Canada

blocks.text: Statistics Canada figures show police-reported hate crimes targeting Muslims across Canada rose by roughly 173 per cent between 2020 and 2024, from 84 incidents to 229.
In June, a Victoria imam said he was assaulted outside his home by a man who told him to "go back to your country."

National Council of Canadian Muslims CEO Stephen Brown is seen in a file photo. The NCCM says it will engage in 'good-faith' conversations with the B.C. Conservatives, 'but Islamophobia must be addressed.' (Ivanoh Demers/CBC)
"We will engage in good-faith conversation with the B.C. Conservatives about these troubling revelations, but Islamophobia must be addressed," the NCCM wrote.
"This must be a bipartisan commitment."
Criticism and response

B.C. NDP Leader David Eby spoke to reporters Saturday morning from Courtenay, B.C., saying Merrifield’s posts highlighted by the NCCM were "so hateful, directed to a very specific religious community in our province," and deserved consequences.
He said if Muslims practising Islam in B.C. can be targeted by the campaign director of a major political party, then "no community in this province is safe."
"[Doerkson] has to remove her," Eby said.
CBC News asked B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson for a statement but did not receive one before publication.
The B.C. Conservative Party replied to a request for comment with a statement from Zeeshan Wahla, its candidate for Surrey City Centre.
Wahla said the language used in Merrifield’s original post from several months ago was "unacceptable," but said it was clear her reaction was "informed by her past sexual trauma."
He said the difference between Agou being dropped over his posts and Merrifield’s situation comes down to the former candidate "inciting violence," while Merrifield was "reacting to violence."

CentreBC Leader Elenore Sturko, in a video posted to Instagram Friday, said just a day after the B.C. Conservatives fired a candidate over "racist, deplorable garbage on the internet," past posts from another member of the campaign team had come to light.
"It’s the same old people and the same old Conservative party," she said.
Sturko said if Doerkson "can’t stand up for all British Columbians," then he should not "stand up and ask to be made premier."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Arden McLeod, from Vancouver, is an associate producer with CBC News. He has a passion for community storytelling, local news, and reflecting the values of B.C. He graduated from the British Columbia Institute of Technology's broadcast and online journalism program. You can reach him at Arden.McLeod@cbc.ca.
