articles.title: Isaias weakens to post-tropical cyclone after striking Florida panhandle
articles.summary:
Nearly a million people are without power in Florida, Alabama and Georgia as rain and flooding remain a concern

Isaias weakened on Saturday to a post-tropical cyclone after

blocks.text: Isaias weakened on Saturday to a post-tropical cyclone after striking Florida’s panhandle as a category 2 hurricane the previous night, though it still posed flooding and tornado threats as it moved inland.
More than 868,000 customers were without power across Florida, Alabama and Georgia on early Saturday as those in the path of the storm began the cleanup process, according to PowerOutage.us.

Although storm surge and tropical storm warnings associated with Isaias had been discontinued, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) warned there would still likely be “considerable impacts” associated with Isaias across much of southern Alabama, Florida’s panhandle and south-western Georgia.

“Flash, urban and river flooding is possible across the region,” the NHC said in a Saturday-morning advisory, adding that there was a considerable potential for flash flooding and landslides across the southern Appalachians. “A risk for tornadoes will persist … through [Saturday] afternoon across parts of the eastern Florida panhandle, Georgia and the Carolinas.”

Isaias through Sunday is expected to produce rainfall amounts of 4-8in across southern Alabama, Florida’s panhandle and Big Bend regions, and south-west Georgia. Localized totals up to 15in are possible, particularly within rain bands across the Florida panhandle and Big Bend.

Across much of the remainder of the south-east US, rainfall amounts of 2-5in are expected, and localized higher amounts up to 10in are possible, especially across the southern Appalachians and coastal Carolinas.

Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, on Friday as a potent category 2 hurricane. It was an atypically late-forming first Atlantic hurricane of the season and lashed the US Gulf coast with heavy rain, fierce winds and life-threatening flooding.
The hurricane’s maximum sustained winds were 105mph (169km/h) and it was predicted to dissipate on Sunday.
Alabama’s governor, Kay Ivey, warned of “possible spinoff tornadoes” and asked residents to “prepare for the worst”.

“Right now, we are worried about strong winds, heavy rain and possible spinoff tornadoes in certain parts of the state,” Ivey said. “As we approach the weekend and any travel plans, make sure you have reliable information as conditions develop. We often hear in emergency management: Hope for the best. Prepare for the worst.
“That is the approach we need with this particular storm system.”

Florida’s governor, Ron DeSantis, said in an interview with Fox News on Saturday morning that his administration had not received any reports of fatalities yet in the state. He attributed that to likely heightened preparation and previous experience with other tropical storms and hurricanes.
“We’re a peninsula in the middle of a tropical part of the world,” DeSantis said. “We’ve gotta deal with these things,” DeSantis said.

And while the stronger El Niño seemed to limit the number of hurricanes in the Atlantic for the year so far, Isaias forming in October with maximum sustained winds of 105mph marked a stark contrast from historical trends.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) predicted a quiet year in terms of hurricanes at the beginning of a season that officially begins annually on 1 June. Noaa anticipated between three and six hurricanes, well below the average of seven. An August forecast from Noaa cut the expected number to between two and six.

Isais is one of the two latest-forming Atlantic hurricanes on record, tying a record set on 8 October 1905. Otherwise, the second-latest date for the first Atlantic hurricane was 11 September – in 2002 and 2013.
None of the eight previous named storms of the 2026 Atlantic season intensified above tropical storm status.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: 'Ragebait' is the 2026 German Youth Word of the Year
articles.summary: Already named the 2025 Oxford Word of the Year, "rage bait" has also been widely adopted in German slang.

image.caption: 'Ragebait' has been selected as the 2026 German Youth Word of the YearImage: Udo Herrmann/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: The 2026 Youth Word of the Year, "Ragebait," was announced on Saturday at the Frankfurt Book Fair by publisher PONS Langenscheidt.
The "Jugendwort des Jahres," or German Youth Word of the Year, is an annual campaign that documents the popularity of new slang expressions.
"Ragebait" (in English: rage bait) refers to social media content that is deliberately designed to make people angry, frustrated or morally outraged.

It aims to drive engagement, since the algorithms of platforms like Instagram, TikTok and X reward high-energy interaction. A post that generates a heated debate through angry comments, or that is widely shared due to the emotional reaction it provokes, counts as high engagement, which leads the platforms to push the content to more feeds.
Shortlist also included 'Peak' and 'Crashout'
"Ragebait" was on a shortlist of three words for the 2026 Youth Word of the Year, alongside "Peak" and "Crashout."
All three terms are borrowed from English, demonstrating once again the language's significant influence on German youth culture.
Around one million young people, aged 11 to 20, have voted since August 28 for their favorite term.
"Ragebait" obtained 36.5% of the votes, followed by 33.8% for "Peak" and 29.7% for "Crashout."

"The close result shows that all three terms have a firm place in the vocabulary of generations Z and Alpha," said Artur Raiser, marketing manager at PONS Langenscheidt, in a press statement. "'Ragebait' held a slight lead from the start," but only by a narrow margin throughout the voting period, he added. "It remained an exciting race for us at the publishing house, too, until the very last moment."
Peak crash out
"Crashout" (used by young Germans as "crashout gehen," or "going crash out") originally comes from the English "to crash out," which traditionally means to fall asleep very quickly due to exhaustion.

But in newer internet slang, popularized on gaming and social media platforms, "crashing out" means having an intense emotional breakdown, losing control of one's temper or reacting with sudden, uncontrolled anger or stress. It is often used with a touch of humor, to emphasize that the reaction might be somewhat exaggerated.
As for the other shortlisted word, "Peak," it refers to something that is the absolute best. In German youth slang, it functions like an adjective: "That was peak football" or "that is peak comedy."

PONS Langenscheidt, a publishing company that specializes in language reference works, has been selecting the German Youth Word of the Year since 2008 — originally via a jury, and since 2020 through an online vote. Offensive, racist or discriminatory terms are not permitted. The multi-stage public nomination and voting process for next year's word will start in the summer of 2027.
"Das crazy" was selected last year, while "Aura" was the Youth Word of the Year 2024.
This article was originally written in German.

October 10, 2026
Germany 'committed' to further Russia sanctions

blocks.caption: Germany has not purchased Russian oil since 2023 [FILE May 2024]Image: Alexander Ryumin/TASS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany on Saturday said it would continue pursuing sanctions against Russia over the war in Ukraine, coming a day after US President Donald Trump announced a temporary US sanctions reprieve on Russian diesel.
"The federal ⁠government ⁠has taken note of the US decision relating to Russian diesel deliveries," government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said in a statement.
"The federal government ​remains committed to the decisions on ​sanctions against ‌Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions," the statement added.
Germany's "support for Ukraine in its struggle to defend itself remains unfailing ... Diplomatic efforts for a peaceful solution continue," he added.
After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Moscow has been subject to round after round of sanctions packages led by the US and EU.
Russian crude and other oil products have been subject to EU sanctions since 2023, and Germany has not imported any oil or oil products from Russia since then.
A spokesperson for Economic Affairs Minister Katherina Reiche said Saturday that "Germany stands fully behind the sanctions packages."
"Our supply is diversified in this area; we are independent of Russian oil," the spokesperson said.
Germany remains Ukraine's largest financial backer in Europe. During a visit to Kyiv last weekend, Chancellor Friedrich Merz reiterated Germany's unwavering support for Ukraine.

In what amounts to a major reversal in US policy, Trump on Friday said he would temporarily lift US sanctions to allow Russia to "immediately" supply over 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to US and global markets.

The move comes as diesel prices reach record levels after the war in Iran launched by the US and Israel sent diesel prices skyrocketing around the world. In the US, the high prices are putting political pressure on Trump's Republicans ahead of the midterm elections in November.
However, despite Trump's claims on social media, it remains unclear how much Russian fuel will reach global markets amid domestic fuel shortages as Ukraine continues to target refineries.

articles.title: Headmaster detained after BBC investigation into alleged sexual abuse of students
articles.summary: Former students launched their own investigation, spending years collecting evidence and testimonies from others who say they were abused by the headteacher.
articles.byline: Endang Nurdin, Rebecca Henschke, BBC Indonesia

blocks.text: Central to the BBC Eye investigation were former students Ziadatur Rahmah, known as Zia, and Sukma Rohana Fajar.
They launched their own investigation after Zia told a former classmate, Yusron Azzahidi, that the headteacher had sexually assaulted her when she was 17. The pair had been star pupils at the school.
By the time Zia confided in Yusron, she was studying in Cairo, Egypt, while he was in Jakarta.
Yusron suggested they gather evidence to support Zia's allegation. Speaking to former classmates, they spoke to Sukma, who alleges that Abah attempted to rape her at the school.
Yusron compiled a seven-page document detailing the allegations, and they gave it to representatives of Nahdlatul Wathan Diniyah Islamiyah (NWDI), the organisation that ran the school.
Thinking the school would support them, the students say that instead, they were pressured to withdraw their accusations.
In a secretly recorded phone call, Abah pleaded with Yusron to protect him and his reputation.
"Cover the shame of your teacher. Everyone makes mistakes, my child," Abah said.
Abah also contacted Zia, who secretly recorded their conversation and shared it with the BBC.
In the recording, Abah is heard apologising, but pleads with her to remain silent.

Following the BBC investigation, Abah held a news conference where he denied all the allegations. He did not deny that the voice heard in the recorded calls was his, but said the recordings were not confessions.

Sukma told the BBC she had been forced to sign a document saying her allegations were lies. She later secretly recorded a conversation with Abah's wife, known to students as Umi. In the recording, Umi tells Sukma that the document was intended to protect "her good name".
The former students eventually resumed their efforts to seek justice, with support from lawyer Joko Jumadi, who has experience in similar cases.
The day after the BBC investigation was published, parents arrived at the school to collect their children, with some travelling from other islands.
One mother said she had begun crying when she heard the news, thinking about her daughter.
"I'm moving her right now," she said. "I absolutely want my child to leave this school."
Yusron said he and Zia, who recently got married, were overwhelmed by the response from former students.
"It was beyond what we expected," he said. "So many people contacted us - on Instagram, WhatsApp. They contacted me and Zia directly, and lots of them were saying, 'I'm a victim too'."
Police interviewed Zia and Sukma, along with the 12 other former students who came forward with allegations of abuse.
"They thought they were the only ones - and it's been really shocking for them to learn, like I did, that they weren't alone," Zia said.
Sukma said she felt relieved and grateful that the allegations are now being taken seriously.
"It's not about revenge. It's more the acknowledgement that what he did was wrong. I'm waiting for the day when he admits that himself," she told the BBC.
Abah has resigned from the school and has said he will respect the legal process.
The BBC contacted Abah and his wife during its original investigation, but they did not respond at the time.

NWDI denied trying to cover up the allegations and said it was investigating them internally. It said it had a duty to protect the organisation from being tarnished by the alleged actions of individuals.
In the wake of the BBC investigation, NWDI vowed to ensure such abuse never happened again and said it would safeguard the rights of students who came forward.

articles.title: Hundreds of thousands lose power as Hurricane Isaias batters Florida, Alabama
articles.summary: Hundreds of thousands of people in Alabama and the Florida Panhandle were without power early Saturday after Isaias crashed into the U.S. Gulf Coast as a dangerous hurricane and left flooded roads…

image.caption: People in Pensacola Beach, Fla., watch the churning ocean as Hurricane Isaias approaches on Friday. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

Hundreds of thousands of people in Alabama and the Florida Panhandle were without power early Saturday after Isaias crashed into the U.S. Gulf Coast as a dangerous hurricane and left flooded roads and downed trees in its wake as it moved inland.
Isaias marks the first hurricane of the Atlantic season
The storm made landfall Friday as a Category 2 hurricane, then quickly moved north through Alabama as its wind speeds dropped sharply.

But the possibility of life-threatening storm surges still loomed for parts of the Florida Panhandle, along with heavy rain and potential flooding for much of the region over the weekend and into Monday.

Isaias was about 40 kilometres south-southwest of Montgomery, Ala., and nearly 170 kilometres south of Birmingham, Ala., with maximum sustained winds of 55 km/h, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) said Saturday.
Forecasters also warned that conditions could stir up tornadoes across parts of the Florida Panhandle and into Georgia and the Carolinas.

items: Hurricane Isaias makes landfall on U.S. Gulf Coast as Category 2 storm

blocks.text: Isaias made landfall near Destin, Fla., as the first hurricane of the Atlantic season.

The storm's rapid intensification was fuelled by record-warm waters in the Gulf of Mexico. The Gulf has seen substantial warming over the past few decades, and experts say the current marine heatwave was made far more likely due to human-caused climate change.

While the warm waters provided the abundant energy that Isaias needed, its formation was also made possible by favourable atmospheric conditions, including weak upper-level winds that would otherwise have disrupted the burgeoning storm.

But just before landfall, upper-level wind shear increased, causing the storm to weaken slightly, dropping it back to Category 2 and making it more disorganized, expanding the area hit by damaging winds.
Hurricane-force winds lashed the Gulf shoreline in the low-lying coastal area known for powdery white-sand beaches dotted with vacation homes, waterfront bars and seafood shacks.
"The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don’t be getting out on the roads," Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said at a news conference Friday.

Roads in Destin were flooded, while in nearby Pensacola, police warned residents to stay off the streets because of debris across roadways. While the extent of the damage was not immediately known, many area residents posted pictures online of downed trees and power lines, and one social media video showed a roof being ripped off an inn in Pensacola.
Some Panhandle counties temporarily suspended emergency response Friday night because of dangerous conditions.

Parts of southern Alabama also were flooded, with officials in Mobile reporting downed trees and power lines. Roads in Houston County, which is in the southeastern corner of the state, were closed because of similar conditions.
More than 726,000 customers in Florida and Alabama were without power early Saturday, according to poweroutage.com.
A man tries to push a car as waves wash over the road on Friday ahead of the arrival of Hurricane Isaias, in Englewood, Fla. (Facebook/Reuters)

Tim Mowry, who rode out the storm from his home in Pensacola, said the wind was so intense it sounded like a train whistle as it whipped through a crack in his patio door. He lost power around 4:30 p.m. but was able to rely on a generator. Standing water also covered his backyard, and parts of his fence were ripped down, but overall he said the storm wasn’t as bad as he expected.
"As far as Pensacola-wise, we really got fortunate," Mowry said.
Mowry said his son, who lives about 15 minutes away, tried to drive to his home after losing power but had to turn around because downed trees and power lines blocked the roads.
Weakened storm threatens region with floods

Despite weakening, heavy rain is forecast as Isaias moves inland, with 10 to 20 centimetres or even more expected through the weekend from southern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle and Big Bend, and southwest Georgia.
The last hurricane to hit the eastern U.S. was Milton, which tore up the Gulf Coast of Florida in 2024.

Isaias also grounded most Friday flights at several airports, including all flights into and out of Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport. U.S. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, scrapped his plans to attend Saturday’s football game between the University of Georgia and the University of Alabama in Tuscaloosa. He said he didn’t want to disrupt emergency response efforts.
In the Pacific, meanwhile, Simon strengthened into a Category 4 hurricane as it approached Mexico’s coast.
Tropical Storm Rachel was also expected to bring heavy winds and rain to northern Mexico and Southern California over the weekend.
With files from Darius Mahdavi

blocks.text: Published October 10, 2026 8:25pm
Vice President Sara Duterte thanked supporters of a movement calling for the release of former President Rodrigo Duterte from the custody of the International Criminal Court (ICC).

“Taos-puso akong nagpapasalamat sa lahat ng mga Pilipino mula sa Netherlands at kalapit nitong mga bansa na nakiisa sa inilunsad na Free Duterte Now Movement sa The Hague noong mga nakaraang buwan,” the Vice President said in a Facebook post on Saturday.
(I sincerely thank all the Filipinos from the Netherlands and nearby countries who joined the Free Duterte Now Movement launched in The Hague in recent months.)

The ICC’s Trial Chamber III on Thursday found the former president fit to stand trial for crimes against humanity in connection with his administration’s war on drugs. His trial is scheduled to begin on November 30, 2026.
Malacañang welcomed the ICC chamber’s findings and expressed hope that the 81-year-old former president would remain healthy enough to face trial.

Sara Duterte said the continued support and prayers for her father’s safe return to the Philippines give their family strength. She urged supporters to continue praying for the detained former president and the country.

“Mga kababayan, patuloy nating ipagdasal ang kapayapaan ng ating bayan, gayundin ang kaligtasan ng lahat. Mahalin natin ang Pilipinas—para sa Diyos, sa Bayan, at sa bawat Pamilyang Pilipino,” she added.

(My fellow countrymen, let us continue to pray for peace in our nation, as well as the safety of everyone. Let us love the Philippines—for God, for the Country, and for every Filipino Family.) — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Operations Plan Germany: How the Bundeswehr trains for NATO collective defense
articles.summary: How prepared is Germany for national defense? The answer lies in the Operations Plan Germany. Military exercises such as "Red Storm Charlie" are designed to put these preparations to the test in…

image.caption: The Bundeswehr conducted exercises in HamburgImage: Norbert Schramm/Bundeswehr

blocks.text: In a residential district of Hamburg at midnight, the streets are quiet and deserted. Suddenly, the silence is shattered: Several helicopters circle the night sky, and flashing blue lights illuminate the darkness. A long convoy of vehicles moves through the streets. Soldiers stand atop armored Bundeswehr vehicles, their machine guns at the ready. For local residents, it is an unusual, perhaps even unsettling sight in an otherwise peaceful port city.

"Red Storm Charlie" is the name of the exercise that will bring parts of Hamburg, northern Germany's largest city, to a standstill for three days. The Bundeswehr, police, and civilian organizations are jointly testing how well prepared they are to respond in a crisis.

The scenario centers on a deteriorating security situation on NATO's eastern flank. NATO troops, represented in the exercise by Bundeswehr soldiers, arrive at the port of Hamburg, Germany's largest seaport, before moving eastwards through the Hanseatic city.

Acts of sabotage and demonstrations, also included in the scenario, hamper their advance. With around 1,700 participants, including 500 soldiers, the exercise held in late September 2026, was the largest of its kind to date.

"Red Storm Charlie" forms part of a classified strategy known as the "Operationsplan Deutschland" (Operations Plan Germany). Through this document, the Bundeswehr is preparing for the possibility of a Russian attack on NATO territory. The Operations Plan Germany is an integral element of NATO's broader defense planning and is closely aligned with the Alliance's overall defense framework.
NATO members in Kyiv: 'We stand unwavering with Ukraine'

In the event of war or a major crisis, not only the city of Hamburg but Germany as a whole would assume a pivotal role as a logistics hub for hundreds of thousands of NATO soldiers, weapons, and pieces of heavy equipment. "This is a highly detailed and strictly classified plan that specifies exactly where NATO allies would arrive in Germany, including which ports they would use and which routes would be required for their transit across the country," security expert Aylin Matlé of the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) told DW.
Germany as a transit country for NATO troops

The Baltic states are widely regarded as the region where NATO considers a Russian attack most likely. In such a scenario, the alliance would concentrate large troop contingents from its 32 member states there. To reach the region, soldiers from southern and western Europe would need to pass through Germany. "In concrete terms, this means that around 800,000 soldiers and 200,000 vehicles would have to move through our country within six months. Those are the calculations," says Marcel Bohnert, a Bundeswehr officer who contributed to the first version of the Operations Plan.

Speaking to DW in a personal capacity rather than as a representative of the Bundeswehr, Bohnert explained: "We must ensure that soldiers can use our roads and ports safely. That is why we take care of all their needs: We arrange accommodation, provide food, ensure their security, and guide them through our transport network."

The plan also covers transport in the opposite direction, from east to west, including the evacuation of wounded soldiers and civilians fleeing the conflict. Its development was commissioned by Bundeswehr Inspector General Carsten Breuer in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. As Germany's highest-ranking military officer, Breuer is far from alone in his concern that Russia could target additional countries. Germany is already confronting a wide range of Russian hostile activities, from cyberattacks to acts of sabotage directed against the Bundeswehr.
German spy chief warns of rising Russia threat
Defense Minister Pistorius: 'Moscow is testing our response'

A new dimension of the threat emerged with the attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August. An explosive-laden drone was deployed there and failed to detonate only through luck. The German government holds Russia responsible. "The threat is becoming more tangible. It is serious, acute, and increasingly visible. This is exactly what the Russian president wants. Moscow is testing our response," Defense Minister Boris Pistorius of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) told the Bundestag on September 23.

The Bundeswehr is also addressing this threat through the Operations Plan Germany, which is continuously being refined and updated. Lessons learned from exercises such as "Red Storm Charlie" are incorporated into the plan. According to Bohnert, the plan also serves as a deterrent: "We hope to discourage Russia from further aggression by demonstrating our strength through the rapid build-up of military capabilities and the highly organized, swift deployment of forces to the borders."
Roads and bridges need upgrading

How well prepared is Germany for its role as a military logistics hub? Matlé identifies one major vulnerability in the country's ageing and, in some cases, deteriorating infrastructure. Germany, she argues, must address the maintenance and repair of the bridges, roads, and transport routes required for troop movements "far more quickly and comprehensively." "Some of this infrastructure dates back to the Cold War and was not designed to accommodate heavy loads or military equipment."

A further challenge lies in striking the right balance between confidentiality and public involvement. To guard against acts of sabotage, sensitive details such as the precise transit routes for NATO troops must not fall into Russian hands. At the same time, the plan can only succeed through close cooperation between the Bundeswehr and civilian society, including local and regional authorities, the police, and relief organizations. "Parts of the plan must be publicly accessible because we need support from society, as well as from ministries and governments, to make it work," said Bohnert.
Could the AfD pass on sensitive information?

The debate over the confidentiality of the more than 1,000-page document recently resurfaced after the far-right Alternative for Germany(AfD) emerged as the strongest party in recent elections in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Security experts expressed concern that the party, which is classified in part as right-wing extremist and is regarded as Russia-friendly, could pass information from the plan to Moscow if it were to assume the office of state premier. The Defense Ministry rejected these concerns, noting that no federal state is given access to the complete document. Instead, the sensitive sections of the Operations Plan are shared only in excerpts and strictly on a need-to-know basis.

According to observers, however, the growing number of hybrid threats is underscoring the need for secrecy. During the "Red Storm Charlie" exercise in Hamburg, accredited journalists were not informed of routes or locations until the very last moment because of concerns over potential disruptions and acts of sabotage.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: ‘Cockroach’ leader among thousands detained in Delhi protest crackdown
articles.summary:
Authorities impose strict lockdown in capital to try to stop rally against removal of 130m names from electoral roll

Indian authorities have placed Delhi under a severe lockdown and detained…
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Aakash Hassan in Delhi

blocks.text: Indian authorities have placed Delhi under a severe lockdown and detained tens of thousands of people, including the leader of the youth-led “Cockroach” movement, in an attempt to stop an anti-government protest.

Thousands of people from across India were blocked from attending the demonstration, which had been called by the “Cockroach Janata party” (CJP) to protest against an exercise that has stripped 130m names from India’s electoral roll.

The Cockroach movement, as well as opposition parties, civil society and student groups, have alleged that the process of “purifying” India’s voter roll was done to entrench the power of Narendra Modi‘s government, and have called for India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who oversaw the exercise, to resign.

blocks.caption: Police detain and carry a protester away in Delhi. Photograph: Manish Swarup/AP

blocks.text: Delhi police denied permission for the protest to take place in the centre of the capital, and in the days leading up to Saturday, officials began to barricade roads throughout Delhi. More than 25,000 police and security personnel were deployed across the city, many pulled from other states.

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder and leader of the CJP, accused the government of being scared of the young people who were rising up in protest. “The mass crackdown on protesters and the shutdown of Delhi are not signs of strength but of a leader terrified of his own people,” said Dipke.

On Saturday morning, police boarded Dipke’s plane as it landed at Delhi airport and detained him, alongside several other senior figures in the Cockroach movement. In a video recorded just before police detained him, Dipke said: “If you think you can stop us by threatening us with jail, then you have it wrong. Put us in jail if you want … but we will keep fighting to protect the democracy of this country.”

blocks.caption: A protester being detained by security personnel. Photograph: Adnan Abidi/Reuters

blocks.text: Others in the CJP movement were detained across India, with arrests and detentions reported to be in the tens of thousands. One of India’s most popular YouTubers, Dhruv Rathee, who has 33m followers and has become a supporter of the CJP, was among those put under house arrest, while Delhi’s former chief minister Arvind Kejriwal was detained at the protest site.

Student groups, who have also been calling for Kumar to resign, had described the march as India’s “second freedom struggle”, akin to Gandhi’s fight for independence. As police began mass detentions on Friday night, Neha Bora, a student leader at the forefront of the protests, said: “History is repeating itself. Just like in 1942, the arrest of leaders could not stop the Quit India movement; this movement will also not stop.” By Saturday afternoon, Bora had been detained.

Over its 14 years in power, the Modi government has been rigidly intolerant of dissent but few protests have prompted such a draconian nationwide crackdown. In major disruption to travel, all trains arriving into Delhi’s two main stations on Saturday were cancelled for 10 hours and almost 50 metro stations were shut. Delhi’s schools and courtrooms were instructed to go online for the day and hotel owners were told to turn away customers.

blocks.caption: Security personnel chase a protester. Photograph: Manish Swarup/AP

blocks.text: Traffic diversions were in place across Delhi and police checkpoints were set up along the main highways from neighbouring states into the capital, with passengers being stopped and interrogated about their final destination. Delhi police told Uber drivers not to drop people near the protest area and said they were “tracking and stopping” bulk orders on food delivery services to Jantar Mantar.
In Mumbai, housing societies sent out mass WhatsApp messages, telling parents to “mind your kids” and make sure they didn’t attempt to travel to join the protest.

Around Jantar Mantar, which had previously been Delhi’s designated protest site and where the Cockroach supporters had hoped to gather, most of the main thoroughfares were shuttered and barricaded, surrounded by police and paramilitary officers. Riot-control vehicles and trucks fitted with water cannon stood nearby.

Buses were used to transport more than 10,000 people who were detained while attempting to reach Jantar Mantar. Paravin Singhal, a 75-year-old lawyer, said he had left home at 5am and shown his court identity card at checkpoints along the way, only to be stopped about 200 metres from Jantar Mantar.

Singhal said he had come to stand with young people fighting to save the country from a “lawless regime playing with the constitution”. He accused Modi’s government and the election commission of using the revision of electoral rolls to influence future votes.

After voting in elections for 50 years, he said, he had recently been told that his name had been removed from the rolls. “How can this happen to someone who has been voting for 50 years? What is even more disturbing is that the government is taking away our most fundamental right – the right to vote.”

Singhal said he would stay put in the hope that more protesters would arrive. “The government is afraid because young people in this country are awake. They know their rights and are fighting for them. That is why the government is behaving like a dictatorship.”

blocks.caption: Police patrol the streets of Delhi. Photograph: Adnan Abidi/Reuters

blocks.text: Amina Minnath, an undergraduate student at Delhi University, had also travelled to the area with friends. They had left before sunrise and navigated the checkpoints. The police barricading of Delhi, she said, had only strengthened her determination to protest.

“These restrictions show that the government does not care about people’s rights,” she said. “This will not stop us. We may be detained, but we will come back in greater numbers. This will not end in a single day.”

The revision of electoral rolls, in a process known as “special intensive revision (SIR), began last year and attracted criticism from civil society groups and the opposition alliance after it emerged that millions of names were being deleted.

The backlash grew when SIR was held in the state of West Bengal and it became clear that Muslims and other minorities, who traditionally do not vote for Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party (BJP), were being disproportionately stripped of their vote.

blocks.caption: A protester is detained. Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPA

blocks.text: Yet it didn’t become an issue of national outrage until late last month, when the Indian Express newspaper published an investigation that exposed multiple irregularities in the SIR process, which had been flagged in more than a dozen internal objections but had been unilaterally overruled by Kumar.

Opposition parties, the Cockroach movement and student groups began to call for the resignation of Kumar, who was appointed by a committee led by Modi. This week, India’s main opposition Congress party, also tried to reach Jantar Mantar to protest but were blocked by police, and the Congress leader, Rahul Gandhi, was detained twice.

This week, the supreme court ordered the Modi government and the election commission to respond to the allegations. A BJP spokesperson said they had “no base, not an iota of evidence” and accused them of being driven by “an irresponsible, anarchist opposition”.

Saturday’s protest follows the triumph of the Cockroach movement in July, when it led mass protests that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister. Since then, India’s youth have proved more willing to criticise the Modi regime and have expressed mounting anger at the obstruction of their freedom to protest.

Many, such as Prakhar Vashishth, who is in his early 20s, remained defiant despite the aggression of Delhi police. He had recently been asked to submit additional documents to establish his eligibility to remain on the electoral rolls.
“We are living in extraordinary times, and young people in this country must come out to defend their future,” he said, as he stood near the police barricades around Jantar Mantar.
“This government will go to any lengths to stay in power, even changing election rules or removing people it believes will not vote for it. But they cannot keep us away for ever.”

articles.title: With power bills already high, Meralco wins approval to raise own fees after 15 years
articles.summary: After its first rate review in 15 years, Meralco has won regulatory approval to raise its distribution charges even after already posting a record P51.13 billion in profits in 2025

blocks.text: After its first rate review in 15 years, Meralco has won regulatory approval to raise its distribution charges even after already posting a record P51.13 billion in profits in 2025

items: Meralco customers will experience higher electricity bills due to a distribution rate increase approved by regulators, marking the first hike in 15 years.
The new average distribution rate will rise from P1.35 to P1.48 per kilowatt-hour, impacting household budgets already strained by inflation and rising living costs.
Despite the rate increase, Meralco reported record profits and continues to pursue modernization projects, while the government is under pressure to lower electricity costs.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Meralco customers will face higher electricity bills after regulators approved the utility’s first distribution rate increase in 15 years, pushing up already-high energy costs and further tightening household budgets strained by rising food, fuel, and other living expenses.

The Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) approved a new average distribution rate of P1.48 per kilowatt-hour (kWh), up from the existing P1.35 per kWh, an increase of around 13 centavos. The actual increase will depend on the final residential rate, though Meralco has yet to clarify how exactly this will raise consumer bills.
The regulator and Meralco has also not mentioned when the new rate will reflect in consumer electricity bills.

Meralco’s overall residential electricity rate already stood at P14.7424 per kWh in September, meaning a household consuming 200 kWh already paid nearly P2,950 monthly. This is before the latest rate hike was factored in.

The distribution charge accounts for only one portion of the electricity bill, alongside generation, transmission, taxes, and other charges. However, it is the portion that actually goes to Meralco to cover its distribution operations and earn a profit.

Meralco’s distribution rates were last reviewed in 2011 and have effectively been frozen since 2015, as successive ERC administrations did not complete regular rate reviews. The prolonged delays kept the utility from raising its distribution charges.

blocks.caption: How do we fix our broken electricity system?

blocks.text: Meralco originally asked for P532 billion in revenue requirement over four years, but the ERC cut this to P342 billion, 36% less than what the energy giant asked for. Even with this reduction, the approved distribution rate is still higher than what customers currently pay.

“We trimmed capital projects that were not yet justified, disallowed excessive operating costs and bad debt provisions, removed contingencies and duplicated assets from the asset base, and used a lower return on capital than what Meralco proposed,” ERC Chairperson Francis Juan said in a statement.

“The approved revenue gives Meralco a clear path to operate more efficiently and to roll out the capital projects needed for a more reliable network, including new substations and lines, modernized metering, and measures to bring down system loss. Meralco will be held to delivering these results,” he added.
Meralco, in a statement on Saturday, October 10, said it had yet to receive the full decision and would need to review it before determining its implications for the company and customers.

“We believe that this will allow Meralco to move forward with greater clarity as we pursue investments and initiatives to modernize our distribution network and enhance service delivery,” Jose Ronald Valles, Meralco’s head of regulatory management, said in a statement, pointing to investments in advanced metering infrastructure, cybersecurity, and other network modernization projects.
The increase comes as inflation soared to 7.2% in September, with faster price increases in food, transportation, electricity, and other household expenses.

blocks.caption: Is a second, stickier inflation wave taking shape?

blocks.text: The higher distribution rate also comes as Meralco continues to earn record profits.
The company reported a record P50.6 billion in core profit in 2025. In the first half of 2026, its consolidated core net income reached P26.5 billion, up 3.8% from a year earlier.

The rate approval also comes just days after Manuel Pangilinan-led Metro Pacific Investments Corporation (MPIC) completed its P12.4-billion acquisition of additional Meralco shares from San Miguel Global Power on Thursday, October 8, raising the holding company’s stake in the power utility to 49.4%.

The shares were purchased at P580.99 each, about 40% above Meralco’s market price that day. Meralco shares subsequently climbed 5.3% to P437 on Friday, October 9, the same day regulators approved the rate reset, although the decision was only publicly announced the following day.

There is also a twist of irony in the increase, as it comes just as President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has been pushing to bring down electricity costs by removing system loss charges that consumers have long been forced to shoulder.
During his July State of the Nation Address, Marcos explicitly called for lawmakers and government officials to focus on lowering energy costs.

“Malinaw din sa pamahalaan ang hinaing ng taumbayan na pababain ang presyo ng kuryente sa bansa,” Marcos said then. (The plea of the public to lower the price of electricity in the country is clear to the government.)

blocks.caption: How much could you save if system loss charges are removed from your Meralco bill?

blocks.text: Among the reforms he pushed for was the removal of system loss on consumer energy bills. Shortly after Marcos made the proposal, Pangilinan, who also serves as Meralco’s longtime chairman, criticized this, warning that the power industry “may not survive” if companies were forced to absorb the cost of system losses themselves.

The government has made limited progress on this front. Beginning with the October billing, Meralco customers will no longer pay the 12% value-added tax on allowable system loss charges, but the underlying charge itself remains firmly in place.

For now, energy agencies are still drawing up plans to reduce these losses. This means consumers will likely continue paying system loss charges for years to come, even as Meralco prepares to collect higher distribution rates. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Russian glide bomb attack on Zaporizhzhia kills at least 15 people
articles.summary: Children are among the victims, authorities say, and more victims could still be buried in the rubble of a large apartment block that was destroyed.

blocks.text: Russia has attacked the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia with five glide bombs, killing at least 15 people including three children, President Volodymyr Zelensky and emergency services have said.

The glide bombs hit residential buildings in the south-eastern city. At least 16 other people were injured in the attack, with more still missing and believed to be under the rubble after the strike on Saturday morning.
Zelensky said 13 other regions had also been hit overnight, adding: "Our responses to [these] Russian strikes will come".
The Russian attacks happened just hours after President Donald Trump announced a deal to import Russian diesel into the US.
Photos and videos from the site of one of the strikes show an apartment block mostly destroyed.
"The ground floor was hit, and the floors above just collapsed," acting Mayor Regina Kharchenko told Ukrainian television, speaking from the scene.
She said more than 80 workers were involved in ongoing search and rescue operations which are expected to continue throughout the day.
The rescuers regularly stop to listen for any noises made by survivors who could be under the rubble.
Kharchenko said Russia had struck at "our very heart" and "our littlest ones" were among those killed, adding that their deaths were "awful grief for their families. For the city."
Zelensky has heavily criticised Trump's diesel deal with Russia, calling it a gift to President Vladimir Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged".
More recently, in his response to the overnight strikes, he said "Russia interprets any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly continue the war.
"Russia must understand that the war needs to be stopped, and for that, it must feel its losses," he wrote on X, external.
Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months, as the war between the two countries drags on.
Zaporizhzhia is a major regional centre with more than 700,000 residents. It is located less than 10 miles (16 km) from the front line and is frequently attacked by Russian drones and missiles.
The latest strikes on the city comes amid a sharp increase in the number of Russian attacks that are causing higher numbers of civilian casualties.
On Thursday, at least 33 people were killed in another Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in Kramatorsk, in the eastern Donetsk region.
The day before, 22 people including five children died as a Russian missile hit an apartment block in the town of Pryluky, east of Kyiv.
According to the UN, the number of civilian casualties in Ukraine jumped by 55%, external in the first eight months of this year.
Russia has also targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since Putin launched a full-scale invasion in 2022.
For its part, Ukraine has attacked Russia's infrastructure - with the latest being strikes on data centres owned by tech giant Yandex.

articles.title: Marcos on Bataan Nuclear Power Plant: 'Too bad they stopped it'
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Saturday expressed disappointment over the government"s decision in the late 1980s to mothball the Bataan Nuclear Power Plant, which was built during his father"s…

blocks.text: Published October 10, 2026 7:04pm

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Saturday expressed disappointment over the government’s decision in the late 1980s to mothball the Bataan Nuclear Power Plant, which was built during his father’s administration.
Marcos made the remarks during his visit to the Singapore Nuclear Research and Safety Institute.

“In 1986, we were already in the first two phases. We were already in that. In fact, that pool of trained professionals...they're still around waiting to put their knowledge into practice,” Marcos said.
“So we never were going to do the last phase that you have. We already managed to do the first and the second, and too bad, they stopped it,” he added.
EXPLAINER: Why is the Philippines turning to nuclear energy?
The late President Ferdinand Marcos Sr. ordered the construction of the plant in 1976 in response to rising energy prices. The facility was completed in 1984.
However, it never generated electricity as the project was mothballed following the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster.
Four decades later, Marcos said public sentiment toward nuclear energy had “changed completely” as households seek lower electricity costs.

“We always worry about… people are worried about safety, and the answer that comes back is that, ‘We don’t care where our power comes from, but bring it more cheaper.’ That’s it. We don’t care where it comes from. So that’s changed completely,” Marcos said.

In his fifth State of the Nation Address (SONA) in July, Marcos said the administration was working to harness nuclear energy, noting its existing applications in medicine, agriculture, water filtration, and plastic upcycling.

“Pushing the envelope further, perhaps it is time for us to revisit nuclear energy production,” he said, expressing confidence that it could “reinforce our energy security and bring down the cost of electricity in our country.”
“Titiyakin nating ito ay ligtas. Titiyakin din nating maipaliwanag nang mabuti sa publiko ang magandang dulot sa atin ng enerhiyang nukleyar,” he added.
(We will ensure that it is safe. We will also make sure that the benefits of nuclear energy are properly explained to the public.)
On July 29, the Department of Energy said it was considering three locations for a future nuclear power plant, with Bataan among the shortlisted sites. –VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Dozens injured and buildings damaged as tornadoes hit Sicily
articles.summary:
Marsala on island’s west coast badly affected after powerful storm approached from Mediterranean

Two tornadoes have struck the coastal town of Marsala in western Sicily, injuring dozens of…

blocks.text: Two tornadoes have struck the coastal town of Marsala in western Sicily, injuring dozens of people, damaging buildings including a school, and overturning cars.
A series of videos began to circulate on Friday morning showing two waterspouts approaching the Sicilian town from the sea as people braced for their arrival.

Dozens of people were reported injured, with at least 11 taken to hospital after being struck by flying debris and shattered glass. Among the most seriously injured was a 70-year-old man admitted to Mazara del Vallo hospital in a critical condition with several fractures.

A school was also hit by the powerful winds, leaving six children with minor cuts and abrasions. At the time the tornado struck, 273 pupils were inside the building, all of whom were safely evacuated. Drone footage showing the aftermath revealed extensive damage to the school, with windows shattered and desks and chairs overturned.

In recent years, people in southern Italy have been bracing for the arrival of a “medicane” – a rare Mediterranean storm with hurricane-like characteristics, capable of producing winds exceeding 60 miles an hour and waves reaching five metres in height.

The weather system developed amid intense heat over north Africa and unusually warm Mediterranean waters. Scientists have warned that rising sea temperatures, driven by the climate emergency, can provide additional energy for powerful storms in the region.

According to experts, record temperatures in the Mediterranean contributed to the freak storm that sank the Bayesian, a super yacht off the coast of Sicily, in August 2024, killing seven people including the tech tycoon Mike Lynch and his teenage daughter.

articles.title: Candidate named Hitler Mussolini elected mayor in Peru
articles.summary:
Leftwing Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores beats far-right candidate in election in remote district of Andes

A businessman called Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores has been elected the mayor of a…

blocks.text: A businessman called Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores has been elected the mayor of a remote district in the Peruvian Andes, according to local election data.
The 45-year-old, who shares two of his names with the notorious European dictators, won the race for mayor of Queropalca, in Peru’s central Huánuco region, and will take office on 1 January.
The candidate from the leftwing Ahora Nación party won 229 out of a total of 663 votes in elections on 4 October, according to the national office of electoral processes.
His closest rival, the far-right candidate Gaspar Osorio, received 204 votes.
Flores, who works in freight transportation, had belonged to Popular Force, the party of Peru’s rightwing president, Keiko Fujimori, until 2025, according to electoral authorities.
Despite the name being associated with Germany’s Nazi leader Adolf Hitler, several candidates with the name have won elections in Peru.
In 2021, the doctor Hitler Saavedra Casternoque was elected to parliament for the centrist party Somos Peru.
In 2018, Hitler Alba Sánchez was voted in as mayor of the Andean district of Yungar, saying during his campaign that he was “the good Hitler”.

articles.title: Rogue Anthropic AI agent gave police fake tip in unsolved murder case
articles.summary: Philadelphia police said the tip was "flagged as spam", but criticised the tech company for taking more than two months to detect and report the breach.

blocks.text: An artificial intelligence (AI) agent, developed by Anthropic, went rogue and sent US police a fake tip about an unsolved murder earlier this year, authorities have revealed.

The Philadelphia Police Department said the tip, sent on 18 July, was "flagged as spam" and not passed on for investigation, but it criticised the tech company for taking more than two months to detect and report the breach.

In a statement police said that the bogus tip came through a public website where people can share information on unsolved murders, and that the AI agent had written that it may have information on a case, and claimed to have seen "someone matching the description".

It is believed to be the first time an AI agent has sent fabricated information to authorities, but is the latest in a series of incidents involving rogue AI activity, including hacking systems or taking control of platforms.
Citing Anthropic, the police department said the AI agent had been running a test that involved interactions with randomly selected websites, when it sent the fake tip.
Anthropic discovered the breach on 28 September, more than two months after the message had been sent, and shut down the automatic testing process that was behind it, police said.
But authorities were not notified for another nine days - on 7 October.
"The company must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city's knowledge," Philadelphia police said in a statement to local media, external.
"The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the city is unacceptable."
The police department added that there were no signs of breaches to any departmental systems, and that its safeguarding processes stopped the fake tip from getting past its spam folder.
But the safeguards "do not diminish the seriousness of an AI system presenting fabricated information as though it came from a person with knowledge of a homicide," the police statement said.
Anthropic this week published a report, external detailing multiple types of "unintended" actions its agents have taken.
Organisations that have been impacted also included several US government agencies including the White House, it said.
The US State Department said the AI agent had filed 20 visa applications using a form on its website, but that they were incomplete and not processed, according to reports.
President Donald Trump recently announced an AI taskforce, which he said will coordinate engagement between the government and all parties, including AI companies, consumers, and religious groups.
Earlier this year, a rogue agent by rival tech company, Open AI, hacked an Australian government website and accessed private data on the country's universal healthcare scheme, Medicare.
In another instance, more than 1,200 OpenAI agents went rogue and started unexpectedly communicating, leading to a large group banding together to hack into AI platform Hugging Face.

articles.title: #CourageON: A river in Cebu remembers
articles.summary: The river has wisdom. If you walk slow enough to listen, then you learn that water always finds a way.

blocks.text: The river has wisdom. If you walk slow enough to listen, then you learn that water always finds a way.

items: Chris L. Villarino, an environmental advocate, shares his experience of a river walk in Cebu organized by the Cebu Citizens Initiative, highlighting the importance of respecting nature.
During the walk, a team leader suffered an injury, which shifted the group's focus from leisure to the reality of nature's challenges, emphasizing the need for humility and community support.

The experience reinforced the idea that environmental advocacy is not just theoretical but requires real engagement with nature, as they prepare for the upcoming #MoveCebu event aimed at promoting civic action and environmental resilience.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Hello, I am Chris L. Villarino. I am a tree hugger, having survived Super Typhoon Yolanda by hugging a tree in Tacloban. Since then, I have dedicated my life around advocacy for the environment by engaging individuals, organizations and communities through forest and watershed walk, wellness and regenerative activities in Cebu. Over the weekend, the Cebu Citizens Initiative organized a river walk together with Rappler’s Cebu-based multimedia reporter John Sitchon, Rappler’s head of civic engagement Jene Pangue, and some friends in preparation for the MovePH roadshow in Cebu. We walked in one of Cebu’s rivers — not the Cebu of malls and traffic, but the old Sugbo, the Sugbo that still whispers.
We followed the water upstream; narrow, overgrown, stones covered in moss, plastic in some corners. But the river is still alive, still flowing. At some point, the water was knee deep.
They say that Cebu used to have a river like this. But now, the rivers are buried in culverts and flood control projects. Easily, we forgot the rivers. But as they say, the river never forgot us.

The river has wisdom. If you walk slow enough to listen, then you learn that water always finds a way. Even when choked with trash, blocked by concrete, the water still finds its way down to the sea. Just like life.
But during this walk, the river taught us its hardest lesson.

On a slippery stretch, our dear team leader had a bad fall; hard, face-first onto stones and sand. In a second, the laughter turned to blood, shock, and silence. He was hurt badly — needed stitches and emergency care.

We cared for him. Good thing we had an emergency kit (thanks Agence France!). We could not call for help. We were deep in the river ravine having walked more than an hour. At that moment, the leisurely walk became real.
And I realized: this is exactly what we did to our rivers.

We walked fast, distracted, taking a lot of pictures, looking at our phones, at the view. We forgot the river is not a backdrop. It is alive. It has sharp stones. It demands respect, presence, and slowness.

We also learned what community means. No one was left behind. Hands reached out. Someone held his head. Someone cleaned the blood. Someone prayed. Someone acted as buddy and walked the way back with him (thank you to our friend Karsten!).
The forest that felt so quiet suddenly felt like family.
He is okay now — stitched, resting, healing (driving around the city doing his work). We are grateful it wasn’t worse but the whole experience gave me an important life lesson.

He fell for all of us, in a way. A reminder that rewilding and re-rivering — whether through watershed walks, building urban pocket forests inspired by Laudate Deum, or carrying out the Handuraw Panaw project — is not just a nice workshop concept. It’s real terrain. It will wound you if you don’t walk with humility, much like surviving nature’s wildest forces as a tree hugger clinging to hope and life during Super Typhoon Yolanda.
Going for a river walk is not just going to a waterfall for Instagram or Facebook. It’s not for the faint of heart. It’s going back to our source.
Thank you Rappler, Jene Pangue, and John Sitchon for walking with us, for being brave, for teaching us courage and walking the talk. Thank you everyone for not leaving when it got hard.

I look forward to carrying this spirit forward into our upcoming partnership with Rappler’s civic engagement arm MovePH for #MoveCebu: Sugbo alang sa mga Sugboanon event this October 14–16, where fellow advocates, community leaders, and storytellers will gather to move together towards environmental resilience and civic action.
The river remembers. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Taiwan to boost military spending to 'deter war' with China
articles.summary: President Lai Ching-te ⁠said in a National Day speech that his country is boosting defense spending to 'deter war' with China. It comes after US President Donald Trump asked Taiwan to pay for US…

image.caption: President Lai Ching-te said his country cherishes peace but will not give up freedom in his National Day addressImage: Ann Wang/REUTERS

blocks.text: Taiwan plans to boost defense spending to deter war, President Lai Ching-te said on Saturday, as China steps up military pressure to assert its claim over the self-governed island.
Lai's government has allocated a record NT$1.1 trillion ($34.5 billion) for defense spending in 2027, equivalent to more than 3% of GDP.
Taiwan's 23 million people face the threat of a Chinese attack. Beijing claims the island as part of its territory and has not ruled out using force to bring it under its control.
"Our aim in increasing investment in national defence is not to provoke, but to deter war," President Lai Ching-te said in a speech marking Taiwan's National Day.

Successive governments have increased military spending as Taiwan strengthens its defenses against a potential Chinese invasion and seeks to demonstrate to the United States its commitment to defending itself.
Lai says China must respect Taiwanese people's right to exist
"We do not seek hegemony, nor do we seek to dominate others," Lai said in his annual address outside the Presidential Office in Taipei, attended by thousands of people, including foreign diplomats.
He warned that peace could not be taken for granted, accusing China of using military and grey-zone activities to change the status quo across the Taiwan Strait.
Lai welcomed talks between the United States and China but stressed that Beijing must respect "the right of the people of Taiwan to exist."
Officials in Washington and Taipei have repeatedly said US policy on Taiwan remains unchanged under President Donald Trump, although some of his remarks have raised concerns in Taipei.
US arms deal in focus as Taiwan awaits Trump's approval
Trump raised concerns in May when he suggested that US arms sales to Taiwan could be used as a bargaining chip in negotiations with Chinese President Xi Jinping, following their meeting in Beijing.
Taiwan is awaiting Trump's approval of $14 billion in weapons sales, including the US-made Patriot air defense system.

At a high-profile summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington in September, trade and artificial intelligence dominated the agenda. One of the most contentious issues, Taiwan, was discussed only behind closed doors.
Ahead of Lai's speech, Taiwanese fighter jets and two Chinook helicopters carrying giant Taiwan flags flew over the capital.

Facing China's much larger military, which continues to expand its arsenal with advanced weapons, including stealth fighter jets, aircraft carriers and a vast array of missiles, Taiwan is increasing defence spending and modernising its armed forces.

blocks.caption: Lai said Taiwan's resolve was about more than its survival in the face of "authoritarian expansion" in his National Day speechImage: Chiang Ying-ying/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Washington remains Taipei's most important security backer

China's Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Lai's speech. Beijing has never renounced the use of force to bring Taiwan under its control, calls Lai a "separatist" and has rejected his offers of talks.
Democratically governed Taiwan faces growing military and political pressure from China, which claims the island as its territory despite strong objections from the government in Taipei.

The United States welcomed Lai's commitment to maintaining peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait. A senior US administration official said that, referring to China, "a routine speech is no justification for aggressive or coercive actions."
The United States switched official diplomatic relations from Taipei to Beijing nearly 50 years ago, but Washington is Taipei's most important security backer.
Saturday's celebrations marked the 115th anniversary of the 1911 revolution that toppled China's Qing dynasty and paved the way for the founding of the Republic of China.
The dispute between China and Taiwan dates back to the Chinese civil war, when nationalist leader Chiang Kai-shek fled to the island in 1949 after his forces were defeated by Mao Zedong's communists.

blocks.text: Isaias, first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season, batters US Gulf coast
More than half a million people were without power after hurricane Isaias wreaked havoc on the US Gulf Coast, with Alabama and the Florida Panhandle being hit the hardest by the storm.

The category 2 hurricane made landfall near Destin, Florida, late Friday, with maximum sustained winds of 105 miles per hour. It weakened to a post-tropical cyclone by early morning, with winds of 65 mph, the National Weather Service said.

blocks.caption: Debris is seen in an intersection in Pensacola, Florida as wind and rain from Hurricane Isaias pass through the area. Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty Images

blocks.text: More than 750,000 people in Florida and Alabama have been left without power, according to poweroutage.us, with outages also reported in Georgia for tens of thousands of customers.

“Things are flying really fast, and I’ve never seen wind this fast before, so it’s intense, it’s scary,” Jonathan Ramos, a 40-year-old government employee, said from his hotel in Pensacola, Florida, where the power went out.
“I don’t recommend people coming down here for fun to do this.”

Isaias intensified into a hurricane on Wednesday night, then becoming the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season.

In the days prior to landfall, storm surge warnings were in effect from the mouth of the Mississippi River to the Suwannee River in Florida. Residents in the affected areas were urged to follow advice from local officials and evacuate if instructed to do so.

articles.title: ‘We’re not asking for luxury’: school protesters in Paris suburb feel abandoned by French state
articles.summary:
Students say they are desperate to get back to class but conditions are so bad that the protests must continue

On a normal school day, Mohammed, 17, wakes at 6am, cares for his younger…

blocks.text: On a normal school day, Mohammed, 17, wakes at 6am, cares for his younger siblings to help his single mother who works as a security guard, then takes two crowded buses and a local train to get to his high school in Sevran, a low-income banlieue town in the suburbs north-east of Paris.

“There aren’t enough chairs or desks to go round, so some students have to stand up,” Mohammed said. “Classes can be so packed you can’t interact with the teacher. In this year’s heatwaves, it felt like 40 degrees in overcrowded classrooms with no shade or curtains. It was so hot my brain couldn’t function.”

The 17-year-old in his last year of high school wants to study management and digital communication at a Paris university. But he said conditions were so poor, he felt all odds were stacked against him and his classmates.

“Some of us have to go months without teachers when absent staff aren’t replaced,” he said. “One class had no French teacher for several months just before the French baccalaureate, so they couldn’t even study all the set texts for their exam. Recently we needed a teacher for a subject taught through English, but when that teacher arrived they didn’t speak English.”

The biggest youth protest movement in the country in decades brought hundreds of thousands on to the streets across France this week demonstrating against inequality in the French education system, decrepit schools, a lack of teachers and large class sizes. Hundreds of schools were blockaded, thousands of teenagers were arrested, and rights groups warned of alleged police brutality, with one child losing the use of eye and another losing a hand.

Mohammed and his classmates, often supported by their parents and teachers, have been at the frontline, barricading their school, the Lycée Blaise-Cendrars, which is in one of mainland France’s poorest départements, Seine-Saint-Denis. They have voted to continue their protests next week, taking their grievances to the local mayor, elected officials and education representatives. Many local politicians have supported their demands. Even the French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, conceded that teenagers had “legitimate” concerns.

Photos on the Sevran students’ phones showed broken classroom chairs, holes in walls, holes in ceilings, mould, buckets to catch leaks, faulty lights. They said basic needs weren’t met, with some toilets broken, others with no doors and often no toilet paper or soap. Video projectors and science equipment were lacking.

blocks.caption: A student shows an example of conditions in the school on their phone. Photograph: Ed Alcock/The Guardian

blocks.text: “We’re not asking for luxury, just the basics to learn in decent conditions,” Mohammed said. “And yet police on horseback charged us when we were gathered to protest outside our school, firing teargas at us and making arrests. It’s so dangerous to be charged by a horse, it could kill you. I just ran, I was trying to help my classmates.”

The high schools of Seine-Saint-Denis, a suburban area nudging against northern Paris, have been a driving force in the protests. The area has the youngest population in mainland France, one of the highest birthrates and the among the lowest average income. Local high schools have a high turnover of young teachers.

Despite co-hosting the 2024 Paris Olympics, and numerous government plans to try to combat long-running problems of inequality and poverty, the area north-east of Paris is still disadvantaged compared with the capital.

In 2005, Seine-Saint-Denis was the starting point for weeks of unrest on housing estates across France, leading to a state of national emergency being declared, after the death of two young boys hiding from police in an electricity substation. This week’s protests have shown that inequality and discrimination has not been addressed in the Paris suburbs and the mistrust between young people and police persists.

Sevran’s Lycée Blaise-Cendrars, with more than 1,000 pupils, has been at the heart of protests about school conditions before. In 2024, students and teachers made a viral video about the state of classrooms, toilets and equipment. The local Île de France region said it had put in place a major refurbishment project for high school buildings. But the teenagers said key issues had not been addressed.

“We’re starting at an unfair advantage because our parents aren’t as rich as others, they can’t buy us books, they can’t take us to films,” said Ilian, 17, whose family has Moroccan roots and whose father is a traffic warden. “We’re missing school during these protests, we risk falling behind in an exam year, we’re desperate to get back into class to study, but the conditions we’re facing are so bad we can’t stop until the government promises action.”

The education ministry this week promised 3,000 teachers to urgently fill gaps, but teachers’ unions expressed doubts and said longer-term plans and more funding was needed, even if the government argues there is little spare cash.

Children’s mental health is also an issue in Seine-Saint-Denis. Ilian has been waiting to see a child psychiatrist for months. At the high school, there was no school nurse and a lack of support staff for children with disabilities, he said.

“The police look down on us as if we’re animals”, Ilian said. “They talk to us with such cruelty.” He told local politicians that some teenagers alleged police had made racial insults against them during protests.

Stéphane Troussel, the Socialist head of the Seine-Saint-Denis département council who met the pupils this week, said: “It’s intolerable that policing is causing part of the difficulties.” He called for the police to stop using a type of rubber-bullet launcher, after they suspended use of stun grenades following injuries. The French interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, has defended policing tactics.

Stéphane Blanchet, the mayor of Sevran, said he supported the school protesters’ demands. He said many in his town of 52,000 people, with a higher than average poverty rate, felt “relegated” and forgotten by the state.

Sarah, 17, who wanted to study at an elite Paris engineering faculty, and whose warehouse worker father was proud she was protesting and meeting the mayor, said teenagers in the banlieue “really feel abandoned”.

She said: “We’ve been surprised and so appreciative of other teenagers in better-off places in France marching in the streets to support us this week. We know we’re disadvantaged and that we have to work 10 times as hard as others to escape discrimination against our postcode. But we can’t learn properly in these conditions when we’re not even guaranteed a chair to sit on in school.”
Students’ names have been changed
